rule_name: Agency Sunset Rule Mandate (Executive Order 14270, "Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American Energy")
agency: White House / OMB (directs EPA, DOE, DOI, FERC, NRC, Army Corps of Engineers, BLM, BOEM)
status: Fully Enacted (in effect; individual agency sunset rules being implemented through 2026)
original_rule_summary: No prior rule -- this is a new process mandate targeting energy-related regulations under statutes including the Clean Air Act, Federal Power Act, Natural Gas Act, Atomic Energy Act, Endangered Species Act, and appliance efficiency standards.
what_changed: Directs covered agencies (EPA, DOE, FERC, NRC, DOI bureaus, Army Corps, BLM, BOEM) to issue a 'sunset rule' by September 30, 2025 (later extended to September 30, 2026 for some agencies) inserting a 'Conditional Sunset Date' into covered existing regulations -- one year after the sunset rule's effective date, unless the agency affirmatively extends it (up to 5 more years at a time, following a public comment opportunity). All new energy-related regulations must include a sunset date no more than 5 years out. If an agency does not act to extend a regulation before its sunset date, the regulation automatically expires and is removed from the Code of Federal Regulations -- no additional agency action or public process is required for the expiration itself. Update: DOE withdrew its own direct final rule implementing the sunset mandate (covering 21 parts of Title 10 CFR) on July 28, 2026, after receiving adverse public comments arguing the sunset process 'bypasses meaningful public input and fails to adequately assess whether the sunsets are consistent with underlying statutory mandates.' DOE will instead proceed through standard notice-and-comment rulemaking on a companion proposed rule it had already filed -- a second agency (alongside NRC) where sunset implementation has hit real friction rather than proceeding cleanly.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Signed EO 14270 personally on April 9, 2025, as one of three deregulatory orders issued that day (alongside the 'Directing the Repeal of Unlawful Regulations' memorandum, tracked separately in this database).

corporate_beneficiaries: Energy producers and regulated industries broadly across the covered statutes -- a structural mandate rather than a single-sector rollback

estimated_health_impact.summary: Severe systemic/structural risk: creates 'rolling regulatory vacuums' where protections automatically expire by default unless an agency proactively acts to renew them within the window -- inverting the normal presumption that a regulation stays in force until affirmatively repealed. Affected regulations may include power plant emissions standards, appliance efficiency standards, Endangered Species Act provisions, and oil/gas leasing rules.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified health impact figure exists for the EO itself, since it is a process mechanism rather than a rule targeting a specific pollutant or practice -- and as of mid-2026, agencies are still in the process of identifying which specific regulations are 'covered' and issuing their individual sunset rules (e.g. NRC's Dec. 2025 proposal found most of its regulations could NOT be sunset because they're statutorily required for safety, and only sunset a small number of unused/obsolete rules). The real-world impact will depend heavily on which agencies let which specific regulations lapse -- track individual agency sunset-rule outcomes as they finalize.

confidence_note: Strong 'process is the harm' entry, similar to EO 14192 but energy-specific and more severe in mechanism -- automatic expiration by default, rather than requiring agencies to affirmatively act to repeal. Worth noting the NRC's early implementation actually sunset very few regulations (found most were statutorily protected), which is a useful nuance: the mechanism is structurally risky, but agency-by-agency outcomes so far are mixed, not uniformly severe. Update: DOE's July 2026 withdrawal-and-restart adds a second data point to that mixed-outcomes pattern -- two of the covered agencies have now hit procedural friction rather than smoothly implementing the sunset mandate as designed.

section_summaries.what_changed: Agencies must give existing rules automatic expiration dates; unless renewed, they lapse from the CFR with no further action needed. DOE has since withdrawn its own implementing rule after public pushback and restarted via standard rulemaking.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: Flips the default from rules staying in force to lapsing automatically, risking rolling gaps in emissions, safety, and species protections.
section_summaries.confidence_note: A structurally risky mechanism, though both NRC and now DOE have hit friction in early rollout -- a real mixed-outcomes nuance, not uniformly severe.

rule_name: NEPA Categorical Exclusions and Clean Water Act Nationwide-Permit Exploration for AI Data Center Construction (Executive Order 14318 and the AI Action Plan)
agency: CEQ / EPA / U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
status: Weakened (not fully repealed)
date_of_action: 2025-07-23 (EO 14318 and the AI Action Plan issued); implementation ongoing through 2026
original_rule_summary: Before this action, large infrastructure projects including data centers were generally subject to standard environmental review: NEPA environmental assessments or full environmental impact statements for actions with significant federal involvement, individualized Clean Water Act Section 404 permitting (with public input) for construction affecting wetlands or waterways, and standard Clean Air Act permitting -- including public comment periods -- for facilities' air emissions, without any blanket exemption specific to AI or data-center infrastructure.
what_changed: On July 23, 2025, Trump signed three executive orders implementing his 'Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan': EO 14318, 'Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure'; 'Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government'; and 'Promoting the Export of the American AI Technology Stack.' EO 14318 applies to data-center projects with at least $500 million in capital expenditures or more than 100 megawatts of incremental power load (or projects otherwise designated by the Secretaries of Defense, Interior, Commerce, or Energy) and directs the Council on Environmental Quality to coordinate with agencies to identify or create new NEPA categorical exclusions for data-center-related construction found to customarily have less-than-significant environmental effects -- allowing qualifying projects to skip the standard environmental assessment or full environmental impact statement process. The order also presumes that federal financial assistance covering less than 50% of a project's total cost does not constitute the level of federal control that would otherwise trigger full NEPA review. Separately, the AI Action Plan directs the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to 'explore the need' for a nationwide Clean Water Act Section 404 permit specific to data centers -- a blanket permitting mechanism that would let qualifying projects avoid the individualized water-quality review a project-specific permit requires. The EPA separately proposed allowing data centers to obtain air-pollution permits without the standard public-comment process. More than 230 environmental and public-interest groups asked Congress to impose a temporary moratorium on new data-center approvals and construction until federal rules addressed energy use, water needs, local impacts, and emissions. The Southern Environmental Law Center -- leading a coalition of nearly 200 environmental, health, and community groups -- filed comments opposing the EPA's no-public-comment air-permit proposal. Seven Senate Democrats, in a letter led by Sen. Adam Schiff, questioned the administration over the potential Clean Water Act nationwide permit, warning it could let data centers avoid individualized scrutiny of their water-quality impacts. As an example of the underlying pressure driving these fights, conservation groups in South Carolina separately criticized a state permit allowing a Google data center to draw 1.5 million gallons of water per day, arguing it prioritized tech-industry water demand over local needs -- illustrative of the water-use concerns the proposed federal permitting changes would make harder to individually review. NEPA itself, signed into law by President Nixon in 1970 and often described as the U.S.'s foundational environmental statute (sometimes called the environmental 'Magna Carta'), requires federal agencies proposing actions like roads, bridges, or energy projects to study their environmental effects before proceeding; a White House Council on Environmental Quality spokeswoman defended the AI Action Plan's approach as 'meaningful NEPA reform to reduce the delays in federal permitting, unleashing the ability for America to strengthen its AI and manufacturing leadership' (AP/ABC News, July 29, 2025).

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Signed EO 14318 and unveiled the broader AI Action Plan on July 23, 2025, directing CEQ, EPA, and the Army Corps of Engineers to streamline environmental review and permitting specifically for AI data-center infrastructure.

corporate_beneficiaries: Large-scale AI data-center developers and hyperscale cloud companies broadly, per the EO's own stated purpose of accelerating this class of infrastructure
Google, named specifically in South Carolina reporting over a state permit allowing 1.5 million gallons/day of water use for a data center amid the same broader permitting-easing push

estimated_health_impact.summary: Environmental and public-health groups warn that exempting AI data centers from individualized NEPA, Clean Water Act, and Clean Air Act review removes public input and case-by-case scrutiny over local air emissions, water withdrawals, and wetland/waterway impacts at a moment of rapid data-center buildout, though no single quantified national health/mortality estimate specific to this policy was identified in sourcing reviewed.

MODERATE confidence that these mechanisms have been finalized and are actually reducing review in practice -- both the CEQ categorical exclusions and the Army Corps nationwide CWA permit were, per sourcing reviewed, still in a proposal/exploration stage rather than fully implemented as of the reporting reviewed for this entry. rule_name: Reopening of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain and National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska to oil and gas leasing, and a new five-year offshore leasing draft program (2026-2031)
agency: Department of the Interior (Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Ocean Energy Management)
status: ANWR Coastal Plain and NPR-A leasing restrictions rescinded and finalized (Oct.-Nov. 2025); a June 2026 ANWR lease sale held under active litigation drew minimal industry interest; the five-year offshore leasing draft program (2026-2031) remains in draft/comment stage as of its January 23, 2026 comment-period close, with no finalization identified as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-10-23 (ANWR Coastal Plain reopened) through 2026-06-05 (ANWR lease sale results); NPR-A final rule published 2025-11-17; five-year OCS leasing draft program released 2025-11-20, comment period closed 2026-01-23
original_rule_summary: The Biden administration had left the Arctic Refuge's 1.56-million-acre Coastal Plain under a 2024 Record of Decision limiting leasing to a small fraction of the area Trump's first-term program allowed, and had suspended Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority's (AIDEA) leases from a 2021 sale. A separate 2024 rule protected roughly 13 million acres of ecologically sensitive 'Special Areas' within the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska by creating a regulatory presumption against oil and gas activity there unless operators could show minimal or no adverse effect on surface resources. The Biden administration's 2024 five-year Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) oil and gas leasing program scheduled no new lease sales in federal waters through 2029, the first such plan in the program's history to include zero new sales.
what_changed: On October 23, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum rescinded the Biden-era Record of Decision on the Arctic Refuge and reinstated the maximum-leasing 2020 program, reopening the entire 1.56-million-acre Coastal Plain to oil and gas leasing and lifting the suspension on AIDEA's 2021 leases. On November 17, 2025, Interior published a final rule in the Federal Register rescinding the 2024 National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska rule, removing the presumption against drilling across roughly 13 million acres of 'Special Areas' and reverting to weaker 1977-era standards; Burgum said the change would 'unlock Alaska's energy potential.' On November 20, 2025, Interior released a draft five-year OCS leasing program for 2026-2031 proposing as many as 34 lease sales -- the most aggressive offering in decades -- across 21 of 27 planning areas, including six sales off California, new drilling more than 100 miles off Florida, and more than 20 Alaska sales spanning Cook Inlet, the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas, and a newly designated 'High Arctic' area over 200 miles offshore; the 60-day public comment period ran November 24, 2025 through January 23, 2026, and the administration later removed the Atlantic coast from consideration after bipartisan political backlash. A June 2026 BLM lease sale in the Arctic Refuge, held while three separate lawsuits challenging the October 2025 decision remained pending (filed by NRDC/Center for Biological Diversity/Friends of the Earth, the Gwich'in Steering Committee, and the Native Village of Venetie Tribal Government), drew just nine bids on five of the 58 tracts offered -- about 72,049 of the 688,829 acres put up for sale -- totaling $3.7 million, with only AIDEA and Alaska-based Hex LLC bidding; neither company has prior Arctic drilling experience. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0510): a separate, non-oil-and-gas Alaska extraction project -- the Donlin Gold mine, a mining venture distinct from this entry's ANWR/NPRA leasing actions -- received its own fast-track federal permitting designation (FAST-41) in October 2025 under the same broader administration push; see the companion entry donlin-gold-mine-fast41-tailings-dam-risk-2025.json for that project's distinct legal mechanism and its own unresolved tailings-dam spill-risk court finding.

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.note: Signed the October 2025 ANWR rescission and the November 2025 NPR-A rule, and Interior released the five-year OCS leasing draft program under his direction, implementing Trump's Executive Order 14153 (signed his first day in office, Jan. 20, 2025) directing agencies to maximize domestic energy development.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA, a state-owned development corporation) and Hex LLC
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: The only two bidders at the June 2026 ANWR Coastal Plain lease sale; AIDEA also had its 2021 leases -- suspended under the Biden administration -- reinstated by the October 2025 rescission.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Oil and gas developers with interests in the newly reopened National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska Special Areas and OCS planning areas (California, Gulf of Mexico, Alaska, Florida)
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: The NPR-A rule removes the presumption against drilling on ~13 million acres, and the draft five-year OCS program would open the largest number of new lease sales in decades if finalized.

estimated_health_impact.summary: This entry documents an environmental/conservation and public-lands leasing rollback rather than a direct human-health standard; the risk is chiefly to Arctic and coastal wildlife and ecosystems, and -- distinctly -- to Indigenous and North Slope communities whose subsistence economies depend on the caribou herds and marine mammals put at risk, rather than to a modeled human mortality figure. The economic case for the expansion is also disputed by the ANWR sale's own results.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: No oil spill or direct human-health incident has occurred under these actions as of this entry; the harm documented is exposure/risk (polar bear denning habitat, the Porcupine caribou herd, walrus, and bowhead and beluga whale habitat, per Center for Biological Diversity and Defenders of Wildlife reporting) rather than a realized event. The ANWR lease sale's weak results (2 bidders, both without Arctic drilling experience, well below the acreage and tract counts offered) are cited by opponents as evidence the leasing expansion lacks the industry demand its economic rationale assumes; that characterization is not independently adjudicated. The five-year OCS program remains a draft as of its comment-period close -- its final scope, if finalized, could differ from the November 2025 proposal (the Atlantic coast was already removed after backlash), so this entry should be rechecked against Interior's final program once published.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the ANWR and NPR-A actions (BLM's and DOI's own press releases, corroborated by Reuters, AP, and Earthjustice) and on the June 2026 lease-sale results (Alaska Beacon, Alaska Wilderness League, Environment America). HIGH confidence on the five-year OCS draft program's proposed scope (NRDC, PBS, NBC News, Earthjustice, Alaska Beacon all corroborate the 34-sale/21-planning-area figures), though its status is a draft, not a finalized program -- treat any acreage/sale-count figure as proposed, not final, pending Interior's final program. The litigation challenging the ANWR decision (three separate suits) was pending, not resolved, as of the sources reviewed.

section_summaries.what_changed: Interior reopened ANWR's full 1.56M-acre Coastal Plain (Oct. 2025) and stripped drilling protections from 13M acres of NPR-A 'Special Areas' (Nov. 2025), then proposed the most aggressive five-year offshore leasing program in decades (34 potential sales, up to ~1.3B acres); a June 2026 ANWR lease sale held under active litigation drew just $3.7M from two bidders.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: Millions of acres of Arctic and offshore habitat -- polar bear denning grounds, the Porcupine caribou herd's range, whale and walrus habitat -- were opened to leasing; the ANWR sale's weak industry turnout raises a disputed question about whether demand matches the policy's scale.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Well-corroborated across DOI/BLM's own releases and multiple outlets for the finalized ANWR/NPR-A actions and the June 2026 sale results; the five-year OCS program remains a draft, not yet finalized, so its final scope should be rechecked.

rule_name: ATF zero-tolerance dealer-license revocation policy and gun-show sales background-check rule (Biden-era gun trafficking enforcement framework)
agency: ATF (Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives) / DOJ
status: Finalized (policy repeals and license reinstatements already in effect)
date_of_action: 2025 through 2026-07 (ongoing rollback, per ProPublica's reporting period)
original_rule_summary: Under Biden-era policy, ATF pursued a 'zero-tolerance' approach to federal firearms licensees who knowingly violated gun laws, revoking dealer licenses for serious violations, and pursued gun-trafficking referrals for prosecution at a higher rate, with a rule addressing the so-called 'gun show loophole' around private/unlicensed sales.
what_changed: The Trump administration reversed the ATF's zero-tolerance dealer-license enforcement policy, inviting dealers who had lost their licenses under Biden to reapply; nearly a dozen previously revoked gun shops had been relicensed and were selling firearms again as of July 2026, with at least 23 stores receiving new licenses after resubmitting applications. ProPublica found a 69% reduction in dealers losing their licenses under the new approach. Federal gun-trafficking referrals for prosecution fell approximately 30% year-over-year. The administration also repealed the ATF's gun-show-loophole rule and shifted hundreds of ATF agents to immigration enforcement work, reducing the personnel available for firearms-trafficking investigations.

primary_proponent.name: Pam Bondi and Todd Blanche (DOJ leadership overseeing ATF policy during the relevant period)
primary_proponent.note: DOJ, which oversees ATF, directed the zero-tolerance policy's repeal and the broader enforcement rollback; individual attribution between Bondi's and Blanche's respective tenures was not fully disambiguated in reporting reviewed.

corporate_beneficiaries: Federal firearms licensees (gun dealers) previously revoked for zero-tolerance violations, at least 23 of which received reinstated licenses
The firearms retail industry broadly, which benefits from reduced regulatory compliance burden and enforcement risk

estimated_health_impact.summary: Public-safety advocates and ProPublica's reporting connect the reduced dealer accountability and trafficking-referral decline to an increased risk of firearms flowing into illegal markets, though this entry does not assert a specific quantified crime-outcome figure tied to the policy change.

rule_name: Presidential proclamations reducing Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monuments by ~90%
agency: Department of the Interior / Executive Office of the President
status: Signed -- proclamations take effect September 11, 2026 (60 days after signing); legal challenges from tribes and conservation groups expected
original_rule_summary: Bears Ears National Monument (established 2016, roughly 1.36 million acres) and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument (established 1996, roughly 1.87 million acres) had federal Antiquities Act protection preventing most commercial development, including oil, gas, uranium, coal, and mineral extraction, within their boundaries. Bears Ears in particular was designated to protect land sacred to multiple Native American tribes. This is not the first attempt to shrink these monuments -- Trump previously reduced them substantially in his first term, a move Biden reversed in 2021.
what_changed: On July 13, 2026, Trump signed a pair of executive orders/proclamations in the Oval Office, surrounded by Utah's full congressional delegation, Gov. Spencer Cox, and state House Speaker Mike Schultz, reducing Bears Ears National Monument from approximately 1.36 million acres to about 121,000 acres and Grand Staircase-Escalante from approximately 1.87 million acres to about 182,000 acres -- a combined reduction of nearly 3 million acres, roughly 90% of both monuments' prior size. The proclamations take effect 60 days after signing, on September 11, 2026. The move is part of Trump's broader push to expand oil, gas, uranium, coal, and mineral development on public lands following his early-2025 declaration of a national energy emergency, and follows a similar, smaller reduction attempt in Trump's first term that Biden reversed in 2021. Conservationists and tribal representatives are expected to challenge the move in court and warn it opens previously protected land -- including sites sacred to multiple Native American tribes -- to extraction industry development.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Personally signed both proclamations in the Oval Office, with Utah's congressional delegation and state officials present, framing the move as part of the administration's broader public-lands energy-development agenda.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Oil, gas, uranium, coal, and mineral extraction companies with interests in the affected Utah public lands
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: Nearly 3 million acres previously under Antiquities Act monument protection would become newly available for extraction leasing and development under the reduced monument boundaries.

estimated_health_impact.summary: This entry documents a public-lands and environmental/cultural-heritage rollback rather than a direct public-health standard; the primary harms alleged are to protected ecosystems, archaeological and cultural sites (particularly land sacred to Native American tribes), and the durability of federal land protections generally, given this is the second such reduction attempt in a decade.

rule_name: Environmental and historic-preservation law waivers for border barrier construction in Big Bend National Park
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- waived for a specific project area, not a nationwide rule change
date_of_action: 2026-06 (initial waiver) through 2026-07-27 (subsequent waiver by Secretary Mullin extending the project area)
original_rule_summary: A body of federal environmental and preservation statutes -- including the National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, National Park Service Organic Act, Clean Water Act, Historic Preservation Act, Migratory Bird Treaty Act, Migratory Bird Conservation Act, Archaeological Resources Protection Act, Paleontological Resources Protection Act, and Federal Caves Protection Act -- that normally require environmental review, habitat/species protection, and preservation safeguards before construction affecting protected federal land.
what_changed: DHS invoked its statutory waiver authority under the REAL ID Act's border-infrastructure provision to bypass the above laws and authorize construction of border barriers, roads, lighting, cameras, and sensors through Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park -- protected federal and state land not previously subject to this kind of border-wall construction. DHS had already awarded a $1.7 billion contract in May 2026 explicitly described as 'for border wall through Big Bend.' rule_name: CFPB overdraft-fee cap rule (Regulation Z / Regulation E updates for large-bank overdraft services)
status: Fully Repealed (CRA Disapproval)
original_rule_summary: Finalized by the CFPB on December 12, 2024, the rule closed what the agency called an 'overdraft loophole' in the Truth in Lending Act for banks and credit unions with more than $10 billion in assets. It required those institutions to either cap overdraft fees at $5, cap fees at a level justified by their own cost data, or treat overdraft lines as consumer credit subject to standard lending disclosures (APR, terms) under Regulation Z. The rule was scheduled to take effect October 1, 2025. The CFPB estimated it would save consumers up to $5 billion a year in fees, or about $225 per year for the roughly 23 million households that pay overdraft fees annually.
what_changed: Congressional Republicans moved to kill the rule under the Congressional Review Act (CRA) before it could take effect. The Senate voted 52-48 on March 27, 2025 to pass a CRA joint resolution disapproving the rule. The House followed with a 217-211 vote on April 9, 2025. President Trump signed the resolution into law on May 9, 2025, formally nullifying the rule. Because it used the CRA rather than a normal rulemaking repeal, the disapproval also bars the CFPB from issuing any 'substantially similar' overdraft rule in the future without new statutory authorization from Congress -- a broader and more durable rollback than a simple rule withdrawal would have been.

rule_name: Public Lands Order 7923 -- 20-year mineral withdrawal creating a 10-mile no-drilling buffer around Chaco Culture National Historical Park
status: Proposed Repeal -- draft environmental assessment published, public comment closed July 29, 2026; no final decision announced as of this entry
date_of_action: 2026-03-31 (BLM formally proposes revocation) through 2026-07-29 (public comment period closes); final decision pending
original_rule_summary: In June 2023, Interior Secretary Deb Haaland finalized a 20-year mineral withdrawal barring new oil, gas, coal, and uranium leasing on roughly 336,000 acres of federal land within a 10-mile buffer of Chaco Culture National Historical Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in New Mexico containing more than 7,500 known historic and 145 cultural properties sacred to multiple tribal nations. The withdrawal followed two and a half years of assessment, 150 days of public comment, and eight public meetings.
what_changed: On March 31, 2026, BLM formally proposed revoking the 20-year withdrawal, opening a seven-day online public scoping period for an environmental review -- far shorter than the original withdrawal's 150-day comment process. BLM published a 140-page draft environmental assessment roughly three months later, after gathering about 70,000 comments during the scoping window, and opened a 14-day comment period (closing July 29, 2026) rather than holding public hearings. The agency is weighing three options: leave the withdrawal in place, shrink the buffer from 10 miles to 5 miles, or revoke it entirely and reopen all ~336,000-338,690 acres to leasing; BLM's own draft EA estimates full revocation could yield the equivalent of more than 2.2 million barrels of oil over 20 years, opening the door to up to 14 new wells. New Mexico's congressional delegation (Sens. Heinrich and Lujan, Reps. Leger Fernandez, Stansbury, and Vasquez) publicly objected to the compressed timeline and to Secretary Burgum's unfulfilled commitment to individual tribal consultation meetings, citing polling showing over 70% of New Mexico voters oppose the reversal. Tribal reaction is not unanimous: the Chaco Heritage Tribal Association, representing five tribal nations, opposes the revocation -- Laguna Pueblo tribal historic preservation officer Richard Smith Sr. said 'when an agency asks tribes for knowledge and then builds its decision without it, the injury is not administrative' -- while Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren supports rescinding the buffer, since many Navajo allottees hold mineral rights and stand to gain drilling royalties inside the buffer zone; some Navajo landowners had blocked access to Chaco in 2023 to prevent Haaland from attending the withdrawal's celebration. No final decision had been announced as of mid-September 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.note: BLM, under Burgum, proposed and is administering the revocation review; New Mexico's delegation says Burgum committed to individual tribal consultation meetings that have not been fully carried out.

corporate_beneficiaries: Oil and gas companies holding or seeking leases within the 10-mile Chaco buffer, and Navajo allottees with mineral rights inside the withdrawal area who stand to gain drilling royalties if it is revoked or shrunk

estimated_health_impact.summary: Revoking or shrinking the buffer would reopen land adjacent to a UNESCO World Heritage Site containing thousands of documented cultural and archaeological properties to oil and gas leasing, a cultural-heritage and tribal-sovereignty harm rather than a direct public-health standard rollback; the administration's own draft analysis quantifies the extraction upside but not any offsetting cost.

rule_name: U.S. Financial Regulators' Participation in Climate-Related Financial Risk Oversight (NGFS Membership and FSOC's Climate-Risk Committees)
agency: Federal Reserve, FDIC, Treasury Department (Federal Insurance Office), Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC)
status: Fully Repealed
original_rule_summary: The Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) is a global coalition of financial regulators that develops shared climate-risk scenarios and analysis to help member institutions assess how climate change threatens financial stability; the U.S. Federal Reserve, FDIC, and Treasury's Federal Insurance Office were all members. Separately, FSOC -- the interagency body chaired by the Treasury Secretary that monitors systemic financial risk -- maintained two dedicated bodies, the Climate-related Financial Risk Committee (CFRC, staff-level) and the Climate-related Financial Risk Advisory Committee (CFRAC, outside experts), created to inform FSOC's assessment of climate change as a threat to U.S. financial stability.
what_changed: In the days around Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, all three U.S. financial regulators still in the NGFS withdrew their membership: the FDIC announced its withdrawal January 21, 2025, and Treasury's Federal Insurance Office followed January 30, 2025, both stating NGFS's work fell outside their mandate or was 'inconsistent with this Administration's priorities'; the Federal Reserve withdrew separately around the same period. Then, at its September 10, 2025 meeting, FSOC -- chaired by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent -- voted to rescind the charters of both CFRC and CFRAC outright, eliminating the interagency body's dedicated climate-risk monitoring infrastructure entirely, with FSOC stating the move would let it 'better focus its attention and resources on core financial stability issues.' Congressional Democrats pushed back on both fronts: over 40 House members, led by Reps. Juan Vargas and Sean Casten, sent a letter demanding answers on the committees' disbandment, and Senate Banking Committee Democrats sent a follow-up letter to Bessent in December 2025.

primary_proponent.name: Scott Bessent
primary_proponent.note: Directed and chaired the September 10, 2025 FSOC vote to dissolve both climate-risk committees. The earlier January 2025 NGFS withdrawals were made independently by the FDIC, the Federal Reserve, and Treasury's Federal Insurance Office as agency-level decisions in the administration's first days, not attributed to Bessent personally, but consistent with the same policy shift he later directed at FSOC.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Indirect: these were oversight/monitoring bodies, not rules directly regulating any industry's conduct or emissions -- the loss is federal regulators' own institutional capacity to identify and track climate-driven financial risk (e.g. insurance-market destabilization from increased disaster losses, stranded fossil-fuel assets), not a direct physical or environmental harm pathway.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No formal quantified estimate exists for the risk-monitoring capacity lost; this is best framed as reduced regulatory visibility into a systemic risk channel, not a modeled harm figure, similar to other financial-oversight rollbacks in this tracker.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the sequence of withdrawals and the FSOC vote -- corroborated by Reuters, Treasury's own FSOC meeting readout (home.treasury.gov), and the Congressional letters demanding answers, which independently confirm the committees were in fact dissolved. This entry combines several formally separate agency-level actions (three NGFS withdrawals plus one FSOC vote) under one entry because they represent a single coordinated policy shift on the same subject matter across the same window; treat each action's date carefully if citing this entry, since they were not simultaneous.

original_rule_summary: The Corporate Transparency Act, enacted in 2021 with an implementing rule that took effect in 2024, required roughly 32 million U.S. companies to report their true beneficial owners to the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), aimed at preventing anonymous shell companies from being used for money laundering, terrorism financing, and sanctions evasion.
what_changed: On March 2, 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Treasury would not enforce any penalties or fines against U.S. citizens or domestic reporting companies (or their beneficial owners) under the CTA, and would narrow the rule's scope to foreign reporting companies only. FinCEN's March 21, 2025 interim final rule formalized this: it exempted all domestic entities and their beneficial owners from reporting entirely, and removed any requirement for foreign entities to report their U.S. beneficial owners. The change reduced the number of companies required to report from roughly 32 million to under 12,000 -- more than 99% of previously-covered entities exempted. NOTUS reported the rollback came despite documented evidence that Mexican drug cartels and Chinese money launderers have used anonymous U.S. shell companies to launder fentanyl-trafficking proceeds, cutting against the administration's own stated anti-fentanyl priorities. A subsequent GAO report found Treasury's expanded exemptions created gaps in the beneficial-ownership information the CTA was designed to collect.

primary_proponent.name: Scott Bessent
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the non-enforcement decision on March 2, 2025, calling it 'a victory for common sense' and framing it as part of the administration's agenda to reduce regulatory burdens on small businesses.

corporate_beneficiaries: Domestic shell-company formation and registered-agent industry, broadly -- no single named company or trade group was identified as the driver in sourcing reviewed

estimated_health_impact.summary: Not a direct health-impact rule -- the CTA is a financial-transparency/anti-money-laundering measure. Its rollback is estimated instead by the scale of exempted reporting (over 99% of previously-covered companies) and a GAO-documented information gap; NOTUS's reporting links that gap to law-enforcement concerns that cartels and money launderers exploit anonymous shell companies to hide fentanyl-trafficking proceeds, a public-safety rather than a direct-health harm.

rule_name: Deregulatory Fast-Track Memo ("Directing the Repeal of Unlawful Regulations")
agency: White House / OMB (directs all executive departments and agencies)
status: Fully Enacted (in effect, ongoing)
original_rule_summary: No prior rule -- builds on Executive Order 14219 ('Ensuring Lawful Governance...'), issued Feb. 19, 2025, which had directed agencies to identify 'unlawful and potentially unlawful' regulations within a 60-day review period.
what_changed: This Presidential Memorandum instructs agencies to repeal regulations they determine are 'facially unlawful' without going through the normal notice-and-comment rulemaking process, by invoking the Administrative Procedure Act's 'good cause' exception (normally reserved for genuine emergencies). It targets regulations agencies believe conflict with 10 specific recent Supreme Court decisions, including Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024, overturning Chevron deference), West Virginia v. EPA (2022, establishing the 'major questions doctrine'), and Sackett v. EPA (2023, narrowing WOTUS). Within 30 days after the review period, agencies must submit a one-page summary to OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) for each regulation identified as unlawful, then move to repeal.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Issued the memorandum personally on April 9, 2025, the same day as EO 14270 (the sunset rule mandate, tracked separately) and an EO on showerhead water pressure standards.

corporate_beneficiaries: Regulated industries broadly across all sectors where agencies determine a rule is 'unlawful' under the cited Supreme Court decisions -- a cross-cutting structural mandate rather than a sector-specific rollback

estimated_health_impact.summary: Severe systemic risk by design: bypassing notice-and-comment eliminates the primary formal mechanism by which public health advocates, toxicologists, affected communities, and other stakeholders can submit evidence or objections before a rule is repealed. This is a procedural harm distinct from any single rule's substantive content -- it changes how rules can be undone, not just which rules.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified health impact figure exists for the memo itself, since it is a process mechanism enabling repeal of other rules, not a rule targeting a specific pollutant or practice. Its harm is best argued as procedural (loss of public input) rather than via a body-count claim. Downstream rules repealed under its authority may have their own quantified figures in other entries of this tracker.

confidence_note: Strong 'process is the harm' entry, similar in category to EO 14192 and the sunset rule mandate. The specific mechanism here -- invoking APA 'good cause' to skip notice-and-comment based on an agency's own legal judgment that a rule is 'unlawful' -- is a distinct and arguably more aggressive procedural shortcut than either of the other two structural entries, since it removes public input entirely rather than just accelerating repeal volume or adding expiration dates. Re-verified with a targeted search for developments since last_verified, CDR batch 2 (2026-09-08) -- no developments found since the last recheck.

rule_name: Dodd-Frank Asset Threshold Amendment (Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act / S.2155)
status: Fully Repealed (legislative rollback of Dodd-Frank provisions)
original_rule_summary: Post-2008 Dodd-Frank Act (2010) required banks with $50 billion or more in assets to undergo enhanced Federal Reserve oversight: company-run stress tests, enhanced liquidity requirements, resolution plans ('living wills'), and heightened supervision, on the theory that failures at this scale posed systemic risk.
what_changed: S.2155 raised the asset threshold for enhanced prudential standards from $50 billion to $250 billion, exempting all but the largest US banks. Banks with $50-100B in assets were exempted immediately; banks with $100-250B were exempted after 18 months (with Federal Reserve discretion to re-impose standards). This was the most significant legislative rollback of Dodd-Frank since its passage.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Primary Senate sponsor and drafter was Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID), Senate Banking Committee Chair. Passed Senate 67-31 (bipartisan) and House 258-159.

corporate_beneficiaries: Regional and super-regional banks with $50-250B in assets, including Comerica, Zions, BB&T, SunTrust, Fifth Third, and Silicon Valley Bank

estimated_health_impact.summary: Indirect/systemic: increases financial system volatility risk, which correlates with mental health and economic-stability harms during downturns rather than a direct physical health pathway. This is not purely theoretical -- the Roosevelt Institute directly traces mechanisms of the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank collapse to the stress-test and liquidity exemptions this law created for banks in the $50-250B range.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No formal quantified mortality/illness estimate exists for this rollback, as is typical for financial (rather than environmental/health) regulation -- the strength of this entry is the documented causal chain to an actual bank failure (SVB, 2023), not a modeled health figure.

confidence_note: This is legislation, not a unilateral executive rollback -- note the mechanism is different from most other entries in this tracker. Strongest framing: cite the direct causal chain to the Silicon Valley Bank collapse as a real-world materialized harm, rather than an abstract 'increases risk' claim. Re-verified with a targeted search for developments since last_verified, CDR batch 2 (2026-09-08) -- no developments found since the last recheck.

section_summaries.estimated_impact: A think tank has since drawn a direct line from these exemptions to an actual bank failure -- Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 collapse.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Legislative, not executive, rollback; strongest framing ties it to SVB's real-world collapse rather than an abstract risk claim.

rule_name: DOE cancellation of clean energy manufacturing/project grants, including admitted targeting by state political identity
status: Ongoing -- a federal court has ruled part of the cancellations illegal; broader rollback (223 projects, $82.9B) continues per a July 2026 BlueGreen Alliance analysis Update 2026-09-03: two specific court wins for terminated grantees, both predating this entry's prior 2026-07-27 verification but not previously named here, are now documented -- in January 2026, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta ordered DOE to reinstate 7 awards worth $27.6 million to Saint Paul, Minnesota-area plaintiffs; on June 12, 2026, a federal court settlement (a separate but related suit led by a coalition including the American Institute of Chemical Engineers) required DOE to reinstate 11 more awards worth $82.1 million to grantees in New York, Oregon, Connecticut, Minnesota, and Colorado, with DOE agreeing not to contest that a 'primary reason' for the terminations was the awardee being in a 'Blue State.' Two further, more sweeping cases were reported still pending as of August 2026: one from a coalition of states including California and New York, and a separate one from the University of California system. FactCheck.org published an August 2026 analysis ('Wright's Hairsplitting Statements About Canceled Energy Grants in Blue States') concluding Secretary Wright's public merit-based framing does not hold up against DOE's own court admissions -- consistent with, and reinforcing, this entry's existing framing.
date_of_action: 2025 (grant cancellations begin) through 2026-07 (court admission and BlueGreen Alliance analysis)
original_rule_summary: Biden-era clean energy incentives -- including manufacturing and project grants funded through the Inflation Reduction Act and related programs -- had been awarded or were pending to hundreds of clean energy and manufacturing projects nationwide, including in Republican- and Democratic-leaning states alike, based on standard DOE project-merit review criteria.
what_changed: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0371): the earliest documented wave in this pattern, predating the political-targeting revelation by over a year. On May 28, 2025, DOE announced it was terminating $3.7 billion across 24 clean energy and decarbonization grants funded by the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law, nearly 70% of them signed between Election Day 2024 and Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration; Energy Secretary Chris Wright stated at the time the projects 'failed to advance the energy needs of the American people, were not economically viable and would not generate a positive return on investment of taxpayer dollars' -- the same merit-based rationale this entry's later DOE court-filing admission (below) directly contradicts. The 24 cancellations included $500 million for a Heidelberg Materials carbon-capture project at a cement plant in Mitchell, Indiana, $330 million for an ExxonMobil clean-hydrogen project, $540 million for Calpine, and $375 million for an Eastman Chemical plastics-recycling project; Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla wrote Wright condemning the cancellations, including $845 million cut from California projects specifically, and called for reinstatement. A September 2025 Washington Post follow-up on the Heidelberg cancellation's local impact in Mitchell -- describing the same May 2025 award, not a separate later cancellation -- found industry figures warning the loss ceded carbon-capture-cement leadership to China and Europe. A July 14, 2026 analysis by the labor-and-environmental coalition BlueGreen Alliance found that 223 clean energy manufacturing and project awards, representing $82.9 billion in investment and 111,765 projected jobs, have been delayed or canceled during Trump's second term, attributing the rollback to Trump's tax and spending law (which repealed or curtailed Biden-era clean energy incentives) and other administration actions reducing federal support for renewable energy and electric vehicles. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0634): on October 2, 2025 -- nine months before the July 2026 court-filing admission below -- OMB Director Russ Vought announced DOE would terminate roughly $8 billion in previously-approved energy funding, targeting projects in the 16 states that voted for Harris; per a House Appropriations Committee Democrats tally, the terminations hit 136 congressional districts, 108 held by Democrats and 28 by Republicans. Vought's own on-record justification at the time was explicitly partisan -- he called the funding 'Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda' -- even as DOE simultaneously offered the same merit-based framing ('did not adequately advance the nation's energy needs, were not economically viable') that this entry's later court-filing admission contradicts; Vought's October 2025 quote is itself a contemporaneous on-record statement of the same political motive, predating and reinforcing the July 2026 court admission rather than being a separate incident. The $8 billion October 2025 figure and the $7.6 billion July 2026 court-admitted figure are not confirmed to describe the identical set of cancellations -- both target the same 16 Harris-voting states, but no source reviewed reconciles the two totals; treat them as two separately-sourced measurements of the same underlying targeting campaign, not necessarily the same dollar total. Separately, in court filings unsealed around July 25, 2026, federal lawyers acknowledged that the Department of Energy canceled $7.6 billion in grants for clean energy projects specifically located in the 16 states that voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election -- an admission that the cancellations were based 'solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state,' contradicting Energy Secretary Chris Wright's repeated public statements that the projects were canceled because they failed to adequately advance national energy needs or represented poor investments. DOE's own lawyers acknowledged using keywords related to diversity, gender, vaccine hesitancy, and COVID-19 to screen projects for cancellation. A federal court has since ruled that the administration illegally blocked billions of dollars in clean energy grants to Democratic-leaning states.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright
primary_proponent.note: Publicly and repeatedly stated the grant cancellations were based on projects' merits and national energy needs -- a claim DOE's own lawyers subsequently contradicted in court filings, acknowledging the cancellations were based on the political identity of the recipient state. OMB Director Russ Vought, who announced the October 2025 $8 billion round of terminations, is the more directly on-record source for the actual political motive -- he called the funding 'Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda' at the same time Wright and DOE offered the merit-based framing.

corporate_beneficiaries.name: Fossil fuel and traditional energy interests benefiting from reduced clean energy competition
corporate_beneficiaries.connection: Clean energy manufacturing and project cancellations reduce competing capacity and investment in renewable energy and electric vehicle manufacturing, indirectly benefiting incumbent fossil-fuel-aligned energy interests, consistent with this tracker's related entry on offshore wind/coal taxpayer-funded rollbacks.

estimated_health_impact.summary: This entry documents an economic and process-integrity rollback rather than a direct public-health standard: the primary harms alleged are lost investment and jobs, and -- more seriously for democratic accountability -- a documented instance of DOE officials publicly misrepresenting the actual (politically motivated) basis for agency funding decisions, which a federal court has since found illegal in at least the $7.6 billion Democratic-state-targeting instance.

Schiff's own press release; sourcing reviewed did not identify a separate, later Heidelberg cancellation distinct from the May 2025 award, so the two records are presented as one event reported twice.

DOE went on to cancel hundreds more clean energy projects worth $82.9 billion under Trump's second term, and admitted in court that $7.6 billion of those cancellations specifically targeted the 16 states that voted for Harris -- directly contradicting Wright's public claims that all the cancellations, including the May 2025 wave, were merit-based.

rule_name: Biden-era pause on new LNG export authorizations (imposed January 2024, pending DOE review of climate and economic impacts)
status: Fully Repealed (pause ended; serial export authorizations issued, including CP2 LNG's final authorization)
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (pause ended) through 2025-10-22 (CP2 LNG final export authorization)
original_rule_summary: In January 2024, the Biden administration paused DOE approval of new LNG export authorizations to non-Free Trade Agreement countries, pending a review of the climate, economic, and national security impacts of continued LNG export expansion -- affecting several proposed Gulf Coast terminals, including Venture Global's CP2 LNG project in Cameron Parish, Louisiana.
what_changed: President Trump ended the Biden-era LNG export pause on his first day in office (January 20, 2025). DOE, under Secretary Chris Wright, subsequently issued a series of LNG export authorizations, including a conditional authorization for CP2 LNG in March 2025, followed by FERC's approval of the facility's siting and construction in May 2025, and DOE's final non-FTA export authorization for CP2 LNG on October 22, 2025, permitting exports of up to 3.96 billion cubic feet per day. Assistant Secretary of the Office of Fossil Energy Kyle Haustveit said finalizing the authorization would 'enable secure and reliable American energy access for our allies.' DOE stated the Trump administration has authorized more than 13.8 Bcf/d of LNG exports in total since ending the pause, exceeding the export volume of the world's second-largest LNG supplier. The same week as CP2's final authorization, Trump administration officials and Qatar sent a joint letter pressuring the European Union to roll back new EU climate and human-rights due-diligence rules, arguing they threaten LNG imports and 'European economic stability' -- a related but separate diplomatic pressure campaign not itself a U.S. domestic regulatory action, and not otherwise documented in this entry.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright, Secretary of Energy
primary_proponent.note: Signed the CP2 LNG final export authorization under President Trump's direction to end the Biden-era LNG export pause; Assistant Secretary Kyle Haustveit is the specific official quoted on the authorization's rationale.

rule_name: Federal support for aging coal-fired power plants -- not a rule rollback in the traditional sense, but a taxpayer-funded market intervention propping up generation capacity that would otherwise face retirement absent federal subsidy
agency: Department of Energy / Department of Defense
status: Finalized (executive order and DOE funding announcement, effective February 2026)
original_rule_summary: Absent federal intervention, aging coal-fired power plants face economic pressure to retire as they compete against lower-cost natural gas and renewable generation; no specific prior rule is being rolled back here, but this entry documents a market-distorting subsidy analogous in effect to other entries in this tracker that redirect public funds toward favored, less-competitive industries.
what_changed: President Trump signed an executive order directing the Department of Energy to issue $175 million (part of a stated $525 million total effort) to fund upgrades at six aging coal-fired power plants across Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, Virginia, and West Virginia, extending their operational life. The same order directs the Pentagon to enter purchase agreements to buy electricity from coal-fired power plants, with the specific purchase volume ('a lot of' coal power, per Trump's own characterization) unspecified in the announcement. The administration frames the effort as boosting energy security and reliability amid rising electricity demand from AI data centers, extending the useful life of existing, already-connected coal infrastructure rather than building new capacity.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump / Department of Energy
primary_proponent.note: The Department of Energy's own public messaging frames the funding as 'keeping affordable, reliable power online,' emphasizing grid reliability and AI-driven demand growth rather than climate or emissions considerations.

corporate_beneficiaries: Owners/operators of the six named coal-fired power plants receiving DOE upgrade funding

rule_name: National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review requirements for advanced nuclear reactor authorization, siting, construction, operation, and decommissioning
status: Finalized (categorical exclusion effective immediately upon Federal Register notice, no advance public participation)
original_rule_summary: Under NEPA, DOE actions authorizing, siting, constructing, operating, reauthorizing, or decommissioning nuclear reactors generally required environmental review, including a written, public assessment of the project's environmental impacts and the possible consequences of a nuclear accident.
what_changed: DOE announced a new categorical exclusion (CatEx) in the Federal Register on February 2, 2026, effective immediately with no advance public participation, excluding the authorization, siting, construction, operation, reauthorization, and decommissioning of advanced nuclear reactors from major NEPA environmental-review requirements. DOE cited the inherent safety features and passive safety systems of advanced reactor designs as justification for the categorical exclusion. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, joined by a coalition of state attorneys general, publicly opposed the exemption as an illegal violation of both NEPA and the Administrative Procedure Act, arguing it minimizes environmental and safety review nationwide.

primary_proponent.role: Federal agency issuing the categorical exclusion
primary_proponent.note: DOE's stated justification rests on advanced reactor designs' inherent safety features rather than a case-by-case environmental review finding.

rule_name: DOE Section 504 New Construction Accessibility Requirements (Rescinding New Construction Requirements Related to Nondiscrimination in Federally Assisted Programs or Activities)
status: Proposed Repeal (issued as a 'direct final rule'; effective date delayed multiple times amid opposition, not yet in effect)
date_of_action: 2025-05-16 (rule published in the Federal Register) through 2026-03-09 (most recently reported delayed effective date)
original_rule_summary: Since the 1970s, DOE's implementing regulations for Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 have required that new construction and significant alterations to buildings receiving DOE federal funding -- including at state and local governments, universities, and private entities -- be built or renovated to be accessible to people with disabilities, mirroring the broader civil-rights mandate that recipients of federal funds not discriminate on the basis of disability.
what_changed: On May 16, 2025, DOE published a 'direct final rule' -- a fast-track mechanism agencies use when they expect no significant opposition, which skips standard notice-and-comment rulemaking -- rescinding these new-construction accessibility requirements entirely, meaning new and renovated buildings receiving DOE funding would no longer be required to meet accessibility standards. Mother Jones reported the rescission was published quietly with no public input sought in advance. Disability-rights advocates, including the Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund (DREDF) and the Partnership for Inclusive Disaster Strategies, along with California Attorney General Rob Bonta's office, filed formal 'significant adverse comment' objections -- the specific procedural mechanism that forces a direct final rule into standard notice-and-comment rulemaking rather than taking effect automatically. Those objections, plus continued advocacy pressure, appear to have contributed to DOE repeatedly pushing back the rule's effective date: originally set for July 15, 2025, then delayed to September 12, 2025, then to December 10, 2025, and most recently to March 9, 2026, per Federal Register notices. A law professor quoted by Mother Jones characterized the DOE action as part of a broader pattern of civil-rights rollbacks, and reporting noted the DOE rescission could be a template for similar rollbacks across more than 80 other sets of agency-specific Section 504 regulations government-wide, since each federal agency maintains its own implementing regulations for the statute.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright
primary_proponent.note: No specific DOE official is named on record as personally directing the rescission; it is presented in agency filings as an institutional DOE action. Wright is included as the department's accountable head, not as a documented personal driver of this specific rule.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Removing new-construction accessibility requirements for DOE-funded buildings would allow newly built or renovated facilities receiving federal energy funding to be built without accessibility features, affecting building access for people with mobility, sensory, or other disabilities at an unspecified but potentially large number of state, local, university, and private facilities that receive DOE funding.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No source reviewed provides a quantified estimate of either the dollar cost/savings to funding recipients or the number of disabled individuals or facilities affected -- reporting characterizes the scope only qualitatively ('thousands of buildings,' per Facilities Dive) without a specific figure on either side of the ledger. This entry states that gap explicitly rather than presenting a manufactured figure.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core procedural facts: the direct-final-rule publication date, the specific mechanism used, the formal adverse comments filed by DREDF and California's AG, and the sequence of effective-date delays are all documented directly in Federal Register notices, independently confirmable at federalregister.gov. MODERATE confidence on the rule's ultimate fate -- as of the most recently reported delay (March 9, 2026), the rule had not been formally withdrawn, but repeated delays in the face of adverse comments leave its final disposition genuinely unresolved as of this entry's most recent verification.

rule_name: ATF classification of forced-reset triggers (FRTs) as machine guns under the National Firearms Act
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- DOJ ceased nationwide enforcement via litigation settlement rather than formal rulemaking; a 15-state-plus-D.C. lawsuit challenging the settlement remains pending, with no ruling identified as of mid-2026 reporting
date_of_action: 2025-05-16 (DOJ-Rare Breed Triggers settlement announced) through 2025-06-09 (15 states and D.C. sue to challenge it); litigation ongoing as of 2026
original_rule_summary: Starting in 2021, ATF classified certain forced-reset triggers (FRTs) -- aftermarket devices that use a semi-automatic rifle's own cycling action to reset the trigger, enabling rates of fire of hundreds of rounds per minute without full-auto conversion -- as illegal machine guns under the National Firearms Act, and pursued seizure and enforcement actions against manufacturers (including Rare Breed Triggers) and owners nationwide.
what_changed: A Texas federal court ruled in July 2024 (National Association for Gun Rights v. Garland) that ATF had exceeded its statutory authority in classifying FRTs as machine guns. Following Trump's February 2025 executive order on Second Amendment enforcement, DOJ's newly created Second Amendment Enforcement Task Force -- under Attorney General Pam Bondi -- concluded that continuing to litigate against lawful FRT ownership 'was not in the public interest.' On May 16, 2025, DOJ announced a settlement with Rare Breed Triggers and the National Association for Gun Rights ending the litigation nationwide, not just within the deciding court's jurisdiction: DOJ agreed FRTs are not machine guns under the NFA, agreed to cease enforcement against FRT owners nationwide, and agreed to return the roughly 12,000 devices previously seized or voluntarily surrendered to owners who requested their return by September 30, 2025, without a state-residency or state-law carve-out. On June 9, 2025, a coalition of 15 states (led by Delaware, Maryland, and New Jersey) and Washington, D.C. sued the federal government in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, arguing the nationwide return of machine-gun-capable devices -- including into states where they remain separately banned, and, per the states' own lawsuit, to some individuals with felony convictions -- threatens public safety and imposes 'irreversible' law-enforcement and healthcare costs on states. The settlement also required Rare Breed to refrain from selling similar devices for handguns and to pursue its own patent-infringement claims against copycat manufacturers rather than relying on federal enforcement. The states' lawsuit remained pending, with no ruling identified in sourcing reviewed, as of mid-2026 reporting; separately, Washington state obtained a carveout from the administration's return plan after suing. At least 15 states had independently banned or restricted FRTs at the state level as of early 2026, regardless of the federal settlement.

primary_proponent.name: Pam Bondi
primary_proponent.note: DOJ's Second Amendment Enforcement Task Force, created under Bondi following Trump's February 2025 executive order, concluded continued litigation against FRT ownership 'was not in the public interest' and negotiated the May 2025 nationwide settlement.

rule_name: Department of Labor's July 2025 Deregulatory Agenda -- 60+ (DOL's own count: 63) Proposed Rule Repeals/Rewrites Spanning Wage, Safety, and Anti-Retaliation Standards Across OSHA, the Wage and Hour Division, and MSHA (an omnibus regulatory agenda, not a single rule)
status: Proposed Repeal (mixed stages) -- the flagship home-care wage/overtime rule was formally proposed July 2, 2025, its public comment period closed September 2, 2025, and as of the most recent reporting reviewed (mid-2026) no final rule had been issued, though WHD paused enforcement against third-party home care agencies on July 25, 2025 pending the rulemaking; the other 60+ proposed changes remain at earlier, individually-varying stages of notice-and-comment rulemaking with no comprehensive public tracker of each one's status found in sourcing reviewed for this entry
date_of_action: 2025-07-01/02 (agenda unveiled; flagship home-care rule formally proposed) through the most recent status reviewed for this entry (2026-07)
original_rule_summary: The rules targeted by this package predate the current administration and were issued independently of one another, including (among others): the Wage and Hour Division's 2013 Home Care Rule, which extended Fair Labor Standards Act minimum-wage and overtime protections to home care workers who had previously been exempt as "companionship services" providers; an OSHA/construction standard requiring adequate lighting in active work areas; MSHA mine-safety requirements; and anti-retaliation and transportation-safety protections for migrant farmworkers. This entry treats them together because DOL itself packaged and announced them together as one deregulatory agenda, not because they share a single underlying rule.
what_changed: On July 1-2, 2025, the Department of Labor under Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer unveiled a deregulatory agenda proposing to repeal or rewrite more than 60 workplace rules (DOL's own count: 63), framed by the administration as eliminating "obsolete" and burdensome regulations. The package spans multiple DOL sub-agencies and touches wage protections, workplace-safety standards, and anti-retaliation safeguards across a wide range of industries. Its most consequential and best-documented single component is a proposal to rescind the Wage and Hour Division's 2013 Home Care Rule, which extended federal minimum-wage and overtime protections to an estimated 2 million home care workers providing in-home services to seniors and people with disabilities. DOL formally proposed rescinding the rule on July 2, 2025, and on July 25, 2025 the Wage and Hour Division announced it would stop enforcing the rule's protections against third-party home care agencies even before any final rule issued -- pausing enforcement while the rulemaking proceeded, though the pause does not affect home care workers' ability to sue their employers directly for back wages, overtime, and liquidated damages. The public comment period on the home-care rule proposal closed September 2, 2025, and as of the most recent reporting reviewed for this entry (mid-2026), no final rule had been issued; the 2013 rule remains legally in effect, though practically less enforced. Other components of the same 60+-rule package, per contemporaneous reporting, include eliminating a standard requiring lighting in active construction work areas, reducing mine-safety regulatory requirements, weakening anti-retaliation and transportation protections for migrant farmworkers, and a proposal to remove OSHA's jurisdiction over certain live-entertainment and motorsports venues (reporting cited NASCAR and SeaWorld as examples). AFL-CIO occupational safety and health director Rebecca Reindel publicly criticized the package, saying workers are "at very great risk of dying on the job already" and that the rollback "is only going to make the problem worse." Each proposed rule change must independently complete notice-and-comment rulemaking before taking effect, so the package's ultimate scope and timeline depend on dozens of separate, individually-contested rulemaking processes rather than one administrative action. Chavez-DeRemer, who announced the agenda, resigned as Labor Secretary in April 2026 amid a personal-conduct investigation unrelated to this rulemaking; Keith Sonderling has served as Acting Secretary since and was nominated in June 2026 to hold the position permanently.

The other 60+ proposed rule changes (construction lighting, mine safety, farmworker anti-retaliation) carry plausible but not yet independently quantified safety risk; DOL's own cost-benefit analysis of the package's flagship component did not attempt to quantify it either.

rule_name: Improving Protections for Workers in Temporary Agricultural Employment in the United States (H-2A Farmworker Protection Rule, 2024)
status: Fully Repealed (enforcement suspended June 20, 2025; formal rescission published in the Federal Register July 2, 2025)
original_rule_summary: Finalized by the Biden administration in 2024, the rule extended new protections to workers on H-2A temporary agricultural visas (about 400,000 admitted annually as of 2025, roughly 15% of average U.S. crop-farm employment): the right to engage in 'concerted activity' with coworkers to improve working conditions, anti-retaliation protections barring employers from firing or disciplining workers for organizing, defined progressive-discipline/termination standards, and wage-disclosure and payment requirements.
what_changed: On June 20, 2025, DOL's Wage and Hour Division announced it would suspend all enforcement of the rule nationwide, directing field staff to revert to the pre-rule H-2A labor-certification process in effect before the rule's June 27, 2024 effective date. DOL followed the nationwide non-enforcement announcement with a formal rescission of the rule itself, published in the Federal Register on July 2, 2025, eliminating the underlying protections entirely rather than merely pausing their enforcement pending litigation.

rule_name: Overtime Salary Threshold Expansion Rescission
agency: Department of Labor (Wage and Hour Division)
status: Complete (effective May 15, 2026)
original_rule_summary: In April 2024, the Biden administration's DOL finalized a rule raising the Fair Labor Standards Act white-collar overtime exemption salary threshold in two phases: to $844/week ($43,888/year) effective July 1, 2024, and to $1,128/week ($58,656/year) effective January 1, 2025, with automatic updates every three years thereafter. The highly-compensated-employee exemption threshold was set to rise to $151,164/year. The rule was projected to make roughly 4.3 million additional salaried workers newly eligible for overtime pay.
what_changed: Two federal judges in the Eastern District of Texas struck down the 2024 rule before its second scheduled increase took effect, vacating it on the grounds that DOL had over-weighted salary level relative to job duties in defining the exemption. The Trump DOL declined to continue defending the rule on appeal and withdrew the government's appeals; the Fifth Circuit dismissed the case on May 5, 2026 without ruling on the merits. On May 14, 2026, DOL published a technical amendment in the Federal Register formally rescinding the 2024 rule from the Code of Federal Regulations, effective May 15, 2026, and reinstating the salary thresholds set during Trump's first term in 2019: $684/week ($35,568/year) for the standard exemption and $107,432/year for highly compensated employees. In practice this formalized what had already been happening since the district court rulings, since DOL's Wage and Hour Division had been enforcing the 2019 thresholds since the 2024 rule was vacated.

primary_proponent.name: Andrew Rogers
primary_proponent.role: Administrator, DOL Wage and Hour Division
primary_proponent.note: Signed and publicly announced the technical amendment, framing it as ensuring the exemption's 'duties, salary basis, and salary level requirements' are 'clearly framed' -- i.e., restoring duties-based analysis over the salary-level test the 2024 rule relied on more heavily.

corporate_beneficiaries: Employers across all sectors who would otherwise have had to reclassify salaried employees between roughly $35,568 and $58,656/year as overtime-eligible, or raise their salaries above the new threshold to preserve exempt status -- disproportionately affecting labor-intensive, lower-margin industries such as retail, hospitality, and food service where many managerial-title but modestly-paid positions cluster in that salary band.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Not a health-impact rule; the relevant harm is economic -- lost overtime eligibility and pay for millions of salaried workers who would have qualified for time-and-a-half compensation under the rescinded 2024 threshold.

estimated_health_impact.caveat: DOL's stated rationale, echoed by the Fifth Circuit's earlier reasoning on the 2019 rule, is that Congress intended the white-collar exemption to turn primarily on job duties rather than a compensation test, and that the 2024 rule's salary jump effectively substituted a bright-line pay threshold for that duties analysis -- a view two federal judges accepted when vacating the rule. Critics, including the bill's Senate sponsors, argue the rescission simply strips overtime protection from workers who would have newly qualified, and that the reinstated $684/week threshold has not been adjusted for inflation since 2019. Both sides agree the practical effect since late 2024 has been the same: employers have been operating under the 2019 thresholds since the district court rulings, so this technical amendment formalizes an already-realized status quo rather than changing day-to-day practice by itself.

confidence_note: High confidence throughout. The rescission, its effective date, and both salary threshold figures are drawn directly from DOL's own May 14, 2026 news release and corroborated by multiple independent legal-alert summaries (Foley Hoag, Ogletree, Stein Adler Dabah & Zelkowitz). The 4.3-million-worker figure originates from DOL's own 2024 rule impact projections, cited secondhand via a Senate office fact sheet; treated as a solid but administration-sourced estimate rather than an independently audited figure.

rule_name: FAST-41 Fast-Track Permitting Designation for the Donlin Gold Mine, Alongside an Unresolved Court Finding That Federal Reviewers Never Analyzed a Tailings-Dam Failure Spill Risk
agency: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers / Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- FAST-41 designation granted while the underlying Supplemental EIS ordered by a federal court remains in progress
date_of_action: 2025-06-10 (federal court remand order) through 2025-10-27 (FAST-41 designation) and ongoing into 2026 (Supplemental EIS)
original_rule_summary: Before this action, the Donlin Gold mine -- a proposed 34-million-ounce gold mine in southwestern Alaska requiring a 471-foot tailings dam to contain mining waste -- had received its federal permits in 2018 through the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' standard environmental review process under the Clean Water Act, without the accelerated FAST-41 interagency-coordination track applied here, and without having been required to specifically analyze the consequences of a large-scale tailings-dam failure spill.
what_changed: On June 10, 2025, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled that the Army Corps of Engineers had erred in its 2018 permitting review by failing to analyze the potential impacts of a large spill from a possible failure of Donlin Gold's planned 471-foot tailings dam, remanding the matter back to the Corps; the Corps began a Supplemental Environmental Impact Statement in response, with federal reviewers only beginning to examine large-spill effects as of early 2026 reporting. Despite that unresolved court-ordered environmental gap, the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council granted the Donlin Gold project FAST-41 coverage on October 27, 2025 -- a fast-track interagency permitting-coordination designation -- citing Trump's executive order on 'Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production,' under which the project's roughly 34-million-ounce gold reserve was named. Donlin Gold's own environmental and permitting manager told reporters the FAST-41 designation would likely not actually accelerate the mine's timeline, but gave the company more confidence in reaching a final investment decision by 2027. The designation is part of a broader Trump administration push adding roughly 10 mineral projects nationally (including Perpetua Resources' Stibnite Gold antimony project) to the federal permitting dashboard. Donlin is planned in partnership with Native corporations holding the land and mineral rights, and proponents emphasize jobs, shareholder payments, and village-service funding; but Alaska Native residents in the region, per an AP feature published August 2025, describe the land and the Kuskokwim River watershed in explicitly spiritual and religious terms tied to subsistence salmon fishing, illustrating the community division the fast-tracked review timeline runs alongside without having resolved. This project and its FAST-41 designation are distinct from, though thematically related to, this database's separate anwr-npra-offshore-leasing-expansion-2025-2026.json entry, which covers Arctic oil-and-gas lease sales under a different legal mechanism (statutory reopening of ANWR/NPRA to leasing) rather than FAST-41 critical-minerals fast-tracking.

primary_proponent.note: His executive order on 'Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production' was the stated basis for Donlin Gold's FAST-41 fast-track permitting designation.
