rule_name: DOT Safety Rule Rollback Package (30+ Actions Across FHWA, NHTSA, FMCSA, FAA, and PHMSA)
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- mix of scrapped, delayed, and enforcement-gutted actions across multiple sub-agencies, not one single rule
date_of_action: 2025-07 through 2025-11 (individual actions dated July-September 2025; ProPublica investigation compiling all 30 published 2025-11-29)
original_rule_summary: A set of 30+ distinct DOT safety rules and enforcement practices spanning multiple sub-agencies: subway/bus driver hours-of-service limits, a motorcycle helmet safety mandate, truck speed limiters, school bus child-restraint crash-protection requirements, aircraft cockpit barrier requirements, freight-train emergency oxygen masks for hazmat crews, heavy-truck side underride guards, seat belt warning systems, automatic emergency braking mandates for trucks and cars, and two pipeline safety proposals (CO2 pipelines and methane-emissions detection), plus the enforcement infrastructure (vehicle-defect investigations, trucking/bus company enforcement cases, pipeline enforcement, PHMSA penalty schedules) that gives those rules teeth.
what_changed: ProPublica identified 30 regulatory actions under Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that current and former DOT officials and safety advocates said conflict with the agency's public-safety mission. Scrapped outright: subway/bus driver hours-of-service limits, the motorcycle helmet mandate, the truck speed-limiter requirement, school bus child-restraint crash-protection rules, and two pipeline safety proposals. Delayed: the aircraft cockpit barrier requirement, freight-train emergency oxygen masks, heavy-truck side underride guards, seat belt warning systems, a pedestrian-protection vehicle safety rating update, and automatic emergency braking mandates. Alongside the rule actions, enforcement collapsed: vehicle safety defect investigations down 50%, enforcement cases against trucking/bus companies down 83%, pipeline enforcement cases down 58%, and PHMSA penalties per violation dropped roughly 98% (from about $475,000 per 30 days to about $8,000 per 30 days). PHMSA Deputy Administrator Ben Kochman, a former director of the Interstate Natural Gas Association of America, personally signed 23 deregulatory proposals -- more than the entire four-year Biden administration total -- including a proposal to triple the property-damage threshold that triggers pipeline incident reporting and questioning drug/alcohol testing requirements for pipeline workers. PHMSA Chief Counsel Keith Coyle previously fought pipeline safety regulations as an industry lawyer through 2023. ProPublica identified 32 total DOT appointees with industry ties, 11 of whom held recent disclosed investments of $12-52 million in transportation/energy company stock. DOT itself, in parallel public announcements, described this as intentionally 'slashing red tape' across FHWA, NHTSA, and FMCSA, and separately told the Washington Examiner it had removed more than 140,000 words from the Federal Register and saved a claimed $1.3 billion across 157 deregulatory actions.

primary_proponent.name: Sean Duffy
primary_proponent.note: Publicly framed the effort as removing bureaucratic obstacles ('We want D.C. bureaucrats OUT of your trucks'); DOT's own press office promoted the same actions ProPublica's investigation scrutinized as a deliberate 'slashes red tape' initiative.

corporate_beneficiaries: Trucking industry (speed limiters, automatic emergency braking, and side underride guard rollbacks)
Pipeline operators (PHMSA penalty and reporting-threshold rollbacks; Deputy Administrator Ben Kochman is a former Interstate Natural Gas Association of America director)
Motorcycle industry (helmet safety mandate scrapped)

estimated_health_impact.summary: ProPublica's investigation aggregated the safety agencies' own prior modeling for five of the 30 targeted rules and found they could together prevent up to 1,000 deaths and 40,000 injuries annually if kept in place -- separate from the harder-to-quantify effect of the enforcement collapse (50-83% fewer investigations/cases across categories) on rules that remain on the books but are no longer meaningfully enforced. DOT's own $1.3 billion savings figure, by contrast, is a self-reported industry-compliance-cost estimate, not independently verified.

rule_name: Wheelchair Rule (Ensuring Safe Accommodations for Air Travelers With Disabilities Using Wheelchairs, 49 CFR Part 382, finalized December 2024)
status: Weakened (not fully repealed)
original_rule_summary: A Biden-era DOT rule, finalized December 17, 2024 under Secretary Pete Buttigieg, made mishandling of passengers' wheelchairs and scooters a violation of the Air Carrier Access Act. It required airlines to accept liability for damaged, delayed, lost, or stolen mobility devices; reimburse fare differences when a passenger's device could not fit on their booked flight; give passengers written notice of their rights when checking a device; and provide annual refresher training for staff who handle wheelchairs and assist disabled passengers.
what_changed: DOT announced on September 29, 2025 (Federal Register notice published September 30, 2025) that it will exercise enforcement discretion and not enforce several of the rule's provisions -- initially reported as covering airline liability for mishandled wheelchairs, fare-difference reimbursements, and written rights notifications, with a DOT spokesperson describing the agency as reevaluating whether those provisions 'adhere to statute or if they are redundant.' A later DOT filing extended the non-enforcement window (through April 30, 2027 for some provisions) and broadened it to five specific provisions, adding the rebuttable presumption for damaged checked wheelchairs and the annual refresher-training requirements for ground staff and flight attendants. DOT says it is pursuing a replacement rulemaking rather than a repeal. The move follows a February 14, 2025 petition to the Fifth Circuit by American, Delta, JetBlue, Southwest, and United, plus trade group Airlines for America, seeking to have the rule -- or specific provisions of it -- set aside as exceeding DOT's statutory authority.

primary_proponent.name: Sean Duffy, Secretary of Transportation
primary_proponent.note: No DOT official is named on the record as personally deciding the enforcement pause; a DOT spokesperson speaking for the department, under Duffy, is the only on-record attribution found in sourcing. Duffy is included here as the accountable office-holder, per this tracker's institution-proxied-attribution convention, not because he personally signed or announced it.

corporate_beneficiaries: American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, United Airlines, and trade group Airlines for America -- the parties that petitioned the Fifth Circuit to block the rule

estimated_health_impact.summary: Removes a period of accountability for airlines that damage, lose, or delay passengers' wheelchairs and scooters, and removes airlines' obligation to reimburse fare differences or give written notice of rights -- while replacement rulemaking proceeds with no set completion date.

rule_name: 2009 Endangerment Finding rescission
status: Fully Repealed
original_rule_summary: 2009 EPA scientific and legal finding, based on peer-reviewed climate research, that greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare -- this finding is the legal foundation obligating EPA to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles and stationary sources under the Clean Air Act.
what_changed: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0500): on July 29, 2025 -- the same day Administrator Zeldin announced this rescission proposal -- the Department of Energy released a report attacking the scientific basis for climate regulation, authored by five longtime climate-science skeptics (Steve Koonin, John Christy, Ross McKitrick, Judith Curry, and Roy Spencer) convened as an internal DOE 'Climate Working Group.' The report was not peer-reviewed before release. Texas A&M climate scientist Andrew Dessler organized a volunteer effort by dozens of mainstream climate scientists (85, per subsequent reporting) to produce a public, point-by-point rebuttal (a 439-page document, per CBS News), submitted to DOE during the public comment period that closed September 2, 2025. The Environmental Defense Fund and Union of Concerned Scientists separately sued, alleging the working group's formation violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act by not disclosing its existence for months and by selecting only members who would produce a one-sided argument. DOE dissolved the Climate Working Group on September 10, 2025 but declined to withdraw the report itself. Despite this scientific groundwork, EPA's eventual final rule (below) dropped the climate-science-based rationale the DOE report was meant to support, resting the rescission purely on statutory interpretation and the major questions doctrine instead -- meaning the report's scientific claims were never actually tested in, or formally relied upon by, the final agency action, even as the administration continued to point to it publicly during the proposal phase. When EPA proposed the rescission in July 2025, Administrator Zeldin marketed it publicly as a $52 billion industry cost-cutting plan; Reuters reported in early August 2025 that lawyers and trade groups representing automakers, utilities, and manufacturers warned the specific legal approach EPA was taking could backfire, creating regulatory uncertainty and litigation risk for companies that had already made multibillion-dollar compliance investments under the standards being repealed, and that the proposed repeal of vehicle standards was reportedly broader than industry anticipated, also covering air-conditioning efficiency testing and battery monitoring/durability requirements, not just tailpipe standards. Separately, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine released a consensus report on September 17, 2025 -- commissioned specifically in response to EPA's rescission proposal -- concluding that the evidence for current and future harm to human health and welfare from human-caused greenhouse gas emissions is 'beyond scientific dispute,' and that the 2009 Endangerment Finding's original conclusion has been reinforced, not undermined, by evidence accumulated since 2009. EPA finalized the rescission of the 2009 Endangerment Finding anyway, on February 12, 2026 (published Feb 18, effective April 20, 2026), removing the legal foundation for EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from motor vehicles under CAA Section 202(a). As part of the same final action, EPA also repealed all GHG emission standards for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty vehicles and engines (model years 2012 through 2027+), eliminating future measurement, control, and reporting obligations for manufacturers -- including retroactively for vehicles already manufactured. EPA's final rule notably dropped its earlier proposed climate-science-based rationale entirely, resting the rescission purely on statutory interpretation (that CAA Section 202(a) does not authorize regulation based on global climate change concerns) and the major questions doctrine. NOTE: this action substantially overlaps with the separately-tracked 'ldmv-ghg-standards-repeal-trump2' entry in this database -- both describe the same vehicle-standards repeal, which occurred as part of this single final rule rather than as two separate actions. Recommend merging or cross-referencing these two entries. Update: on April 8, 2026, Zeldin defended the rescission at a Heartland Institute conference -- a think tank that rejects mainstream climate science -- telling attendees to 'celebrate vindication' and framing the repeal as reversing decades of 'unthinking adherence to liberal politicians and environmental groups' on climate change; Heartland president James Taylor called Zeldin 'the greatest EPA administrator ever.' Environmental groups criticized the appearance as EPA's own administrator publicly aligning with climate-denial advocacy rather than the agency's own prior scientific findings. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0609): a Politico/E&E News investigation, published shortly after the report's release, reported that the report's five authors had undisclosed ties to anti-regulatory think tanks that have received fossil-fuel-linked funding -- Roy Spencer affiliated with the Heartland Institute and Heritage Foundation, Ross McKitrick a fellow at Canada's Fraser Institute and affiliated with the Cato Institute, and Steve Koonin's prior work through the Hoover Institution focused specifically on opposing the endangerment finding. Politico also reported the report drew on outdated or non-peer-reviewed sources and cited IPCC findings selectively, out of the surrounding context that would otherwise qualify them. Industry-aligned advocacy groups (the Competitive Enterprise Institute, WattsUpWithThat) publicly disputed Politico's specific hurricane-related critique as itself misleading, making the report's underlying scientific merit a genuinely contested question between advocacy groups on both sides, distinct from the undisclosed-funding-ties finding, which rests on Politico's own sourcing of the authors' institutional affiliations rather than a scientific judgment.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA itself described this as 'the single largest deregulatory action in U.S. history.' Trump directed EPA to evaluate the finding's legality via executive order on his first day in office (Jan 2025); Zeldin formally recommended reconsideration by March 2025.

corporate_beneficiaries: Fossil fuel producers and fossil-fuel-dependent power generators broadly, as the finding underlies multiple downstream emissions rules
Vehicle and engine manufacturers, who EPA states no longer have future GHG measurement/control/reporting obligations for any highway vehicle, including past model years

estimated_health_impact.summary: EPA's own framing states the rescission will save Americans over $1.3 trillion, though this figure is not broken down between compliance-cost savings and forgone health/climate benefits. Because the endangerment finding is the legal foundation for multiple downstream rules, its fuller health impact is best understood as unlocking rollback of everything built on top of it (vehicle GHG standards already repealed in the same action; power plant standards likely to follow under the same legal theory).

The earlier $52 billion figure was EPA's own framing at the proposal stage and is a different, smaller number than the $1.3 trillion total-savings figure claimed at finalization -- present both as EPA's own evolving claims, not as two independent confirmations of the same number. Multiple health and environmental organizations dispute the underlying reasoning; see litigation status below. Reuters also reported industry lawyers and trade groups -- not just environmental advocates -- warned the repeal's legal approach could create regulatory uncertainty and litigation risk for companies with existing compliance investments, complicating the 'purely a business win' framing. Separately, the National Academies' September 2025 consensus report found the scientific basis for the 2009 finding 'beyond scientific dispute' and reinforced by post-2009 evidence -- a direct scientific rebuttal to EPA's rescission rationale from the nation's leading scientific advisory body, not an advocacy group.

rule_name: 10-for-1 Regulatory Repeal Mandate (Executive Order 14192, "Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation")
agency: White House / OMB (governs all federal agencies)
status: Fully Enacted (in effect, ongoing)
original_rule_summary: No prior rule -- this is a new process mandate. It supersedes the first Trump administration's 2017 EO 13771, which required a 2-for-1 repeal ratio.
what_changed: Requires every federal agency to identify at least 10 existing regulations (broadly defined to include guidance documents, memoranda, and policy statements, not just formal APA rules) to repeal for every 1 new regulation proposed. Also requires that the total incremental cost of all new regulations in FY2025 be 'significantly less than zero,' effectively mandating net deregulation by volume and cost simultaneously. Exempts military, national security, homeland security, foreign affairs, and immigration-related regulations.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.note: Signed personally on January 31, 2025, his first full month in office in the second term; explicitly builds on and escalates his own first-term EO 13771 (2-for-1).

corporate_beneficiaries: Regulated industries broadly across all sectors -- this is a cross-cutting structural mandate rather than a sector-specific rollback

estimated_health_impact.summary: Severe systemic/structural risk: by design, this EO prioritizes repeal volume and aggregate cost reduction over case-by-case risk assessment of which specific protections get cut, creating pressure to eliminate rules based on their cost to industry rather than their public health or safety value.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified health impact figure exists for the EO itself, since it is a process mandate rather than a rule targeting a specific pollutant, product, or practice -- its harm is best argued structurally (the mechanism itself deprioritizes public-health benefit analysis) rather than with a body-count claim. Downstream rules repealed under its authority may have their own quantified figures (see other entries in this tracker).

confidence_note: This is one of the strongest 'process is the harm' entries in the tracker -- the EO's text itself, not a critic's characterization, establishes that repeal volume/cost savings are the stated goal, independent of the safety value of any given rule. Good for framing a systemic argument distinct from any single rollback.

rule_name: EPA's March 12, 2025 Announcement of 31 Simultaneous Deregulatory Actions -- 'The Greatest Day of Deregulation in Our Nation's History'
status: Announced (each of the 31 individual actions proceeded on its own separate rulemaking timeline afterward -- see the specific-rule entries this announcement launched)
original_rule_summary: Before this announcement, EPA administered dozens of separate Biden-era and earlier environmental regulations across air, water, and climate policy -- including the 2009 endangerment finding underpinning EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gases, power-plant and vehicle emissions standards, mercury and toxics limits, PFAS drinking-water standards, the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, the Clean Air Act's interstate 'Good Neighbor' pollution provision, and the agency's practice of weighing health costs from storms, wildfires, and droughts in its own rulemaking.
what_changed: On March 12, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced 31 deregulatory actions in a single day, calling it 'the greatest day of deregulation our nation has seen' and stating the agency was 'driving a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion to drive down the cost of living.' The targeted list spanned the 2009 endangerment finding for greenhouse gases, vehicle emissions/fuel-economy standards, coal-fired power-plant carbon and mercury limits, oil-and-gas-sector methane rules, coal-plant wastewater discharge limits, the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, the Clean Air Act's interstate 'Good Neighbor' provision, and EPA's practice of considering climate-linked health costs (from storms, wildfires, droughts) in its own cost-benefit rulemaking, among other targets. Framed as a single package, the announcement functioned as a roadmap rather than a set of completed actions -- each individual rule then proceeded on its own separate proposal/finalization timeline over the following year, several of which this database tracks as distinct entries (see cross-references below). The announcement itself, not any single rule within it, is documented here because of its scale, its status as the stated organizing framework for the administration's broader environmental deregulatory program, and the bipartisan condemnation it drew on its own terms.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced all 31 actions in a single press event, framing them explicitly in ideological terms ('a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion') rather than as individually justified technical rulemakings.

corporate_beneficiaries: Fossil-fuel and coal-power-generation industries broadly, per EcoWatch's framing of the announcement as 'the day Trump's Big Oil megadonors paid for' -- a characterization from Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, not an EPA-sourced or independently quantified claim

estimated_health_impact.summary: Because this entry documents the announcement rather than any single finalized rule, no agency or independent body has produced a combined health-impact estimate for all 31 actions together; each constituent rule's own estimated health impact (where finalized and quantifiable) is tracked in that rule's separate entry in this database. Update 2025-11-19 (added 2026-09-11): a ProPublica/Guardian analysis has since produced a cross-policy mortality projection spanning this announcement plus other 2025 climate/energy actions (OBBBA tax-credit repeal, drilling expansion) -- see propublica-climate-rollback-heat-death-projection-2025.json for that aggregate estimate; it is not repeated here to avoid double-counting.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: This entry intentionally carries no aggregate figures to avoid double-counting harms already estimated individually in the specific-rule entries this announcement launched. See those entries for quantified figures.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the announcement's content and Zeldin's own quotes -- corroborated across EcoWatch, NPR, the EPA's own press materials, and multiple law-firm client alerts (Taft, Holland & Knight, Babst Calland) that treat it as a significant, citable regulatory event. The bipartisan-condemnation framing is well-sourced to on-record quotes from former EPA Administrators Gina McCarthy (Obama-era, calling it 'the most disastrous day in EPA history') and Christine Todd Whitman (George W. rule_name: EPA's Decision to Stop Monetizing Public-Health Benefits in Air Pollution Rulemaking
status: Finalized -- adopted as part of a new final rule on power-plant emissions, with EPA stating it will apply the same non-monetization approach to future air-pollution rulemakings generally
original_rule_summary: For decades, EPA's cost-benefit analyses for air-pollution rules have assigned a dollar value to avoided deaths, illnesses, and hospitalizations from reduced ozone and fine-particulate (PM2.5) pollution, using an established methodology (the 'value of a statistical life' framework) to weigh regulatory costs against quantified public-health benefits -- these monetized health benefits have historically been the largest benefit category justifying stricter air-pollution standards.
what_changed: On January 12, 2026, EPA announced it would no longer assign an economic value to lives saved or health improved when justifying air-pollution rules, unveiling a final rule under the Clean Air Act that simultaneously revised (weakened) nitrogen oxide (NOx) emission limits for new gas-burning turbines at power plants and industrial facilities. EPA's new regulatory language stated the agency would stop monetizing public-health benefits from reduced ozone and fine-particulate pollution because, in EPA's words, its 'historical analytical practices often provided the public with false precision and confidence' -- even while the agency's own rule acknowledged that these pollutants contribute to pulmonary disease, heart attacks, and premature death. EPA characterized the change as applying beyond this single rule to its air-pollution rulemaking generally going forward, meaning future rules would be justified without counting the dollar value of avoided illness and death as a benefit, structurally shifting the cost-benefit balance toward looser standards across the agency's future air-pollution decisions.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA finalized the policy change under Zeldin's leadership as part of the same broader deregulatory program including the March 2025 31-rule announcement and the February 2026 endangerment-finding rescission.

corporate_beneficiaries: Power plant and industrial-facility operators facing future air-pollution rulemakings, whose compliance costs would no longer be weighed against a monetized health-benefit figure

estimated_health_impact.summary: This is a methodological change to how EPA justifies air-pollution rules, not a rule permitting a specific quantity of additional pollution -- but because monetized health benefits have historically been the dominant benefit category in EPA's cost-benefit analyses, removing them structurally weakens the case for stricter future air-pollution standards across the board, independent of any single rule's specific numbers.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No source reviewed quantifies an aggregate future health impact from this methodological shift, since its effect depends on which specific future rules it is applied to and how; the entry documents the structural policy change itself, which multiple public-health and environmental-law observers (Human Rights Watch, EDF, the University of Chicago's Air Quality Life Index project) characterize as highly consequential precisely because of its generality.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- corroborated across The Washington Post, NBC News, Human Rights Watch, OPB/GBH (NPR member stations), the Environmental Defense Fund, and the University of Chicago's Air Quality Life Index project, all reporting the same January 12, 2026 announcement and EPA's own quoted 'false precision and confidence' rationale.
short_summary: EPA said it will stop assigning a dollar value to lives saved when justifying air-pollution rules, a structural policy shift.

rule_name: EPA civil/criminal enforcement and compliance monitoring of environmental laws against polluters -- including Clean Water Act violations specifically (not a specific rule -- documents an enforcement-practice collapse achieved without formally repealing underlying statutes/rules)
agency: EPA / DOJ (DOJ files civil enforcement referrals on EPA's behalf)
status: Finalized as a completed calendar-year figure (2025); ongoing as an enforcement posture into 2026
original_rule_summary: Historically, DOJ files civil court complaints on EPA's behalf against companies found violating environmental laws (Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and related statutes), a routine enforcement mechanism independent of any specific rule needing to change.
what_changed: Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0509: The New York Times reported August 8, 2025, citing an earlier six-month analysis by the same watchdog group later cited below, that DOJ filed just 11 civil lawsuits against major polluters in the first six full months of Trump's second term, compared with 30 in the same period under Biden, and reached only 18 settlements in such cases compared with 53 under Biden over the same span; the same reporting described environmental-enforcement staffing at DOJ as down roughly a third. The Environmental Integrity Project, an independent watchdog group, found DOJ filed just 16 civil enforcement complaints on EPA's behalf in 2025 -- the lowest first-year enforcement total on record, below even Trump's own first term (2017), representing a 76% decline compared to the Biden administration's first year and an 81% decline compared to Trump's first term. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin's agency disputed the findings in response to NPR's reporting. The decline was achieved through enforcement-referral practice rather than any formal rule repeal, meaning the underlying environmental standards remain on the books but are not being actively enforced against violators at anything close to historical rates. The same February 5, 2026 Environmental Integrity Project report that documented the 16-complaint civil-referral figure also found broader, budget-driven enforcement cuts across the agency: a 30% reduction in civil enforcement funding (from $201.3 million to $61.1 million -- figures as reported, though the described cut and the before/after totals do not arithmetically match and should be verified against the report directly before citing the dollar figures in debate), a 49% cut to criminal enforcement funding (from $60 million to $29.6 million), and a 35% reduction in compliance-monitoring funding. Water-infrastructure funding was cut by approximately 90%. On Clean Water Act enforcement specifically, the report found 3,001 facilities nationwide in 'significant noncompliance' with the Act for three or more years as of January 2026, and only 12% of facilities with air-pollution violations received any enforcement action over the prior year (the reviewed reporting did not isolate an equivalent percentage specific to water-pollution violations). Total EPA penalties collected through September 2025 were $41 million, $8 million less than the same period in the first year of the Biden administration after adjusting for inflation -- described as the weakest EPA enforcement performance in 20 years across seven separate enforcement categories tracked in the report.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA disputed the Environmental Integrity Project's findings when NPR sought comment, but did not provide an alternative enforcement-count figure in the reporting reviewed.

corporate_beneficiaries: Industrial polluters and regulated entities facing substantially reduced likelihood of federal civil enforcement action for Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and related violations

estimated_health_impact.summary: Earthjustice's analysis argues the enforcement collapse undercuts Zeldin's public statements characterizing EPA enforcement as still serious, since sharply reduced referral volume means fewer violations are being formally addressed regardless of the underlying rules' continued existence -- a form of de facto deregulation achieved without any of the formal rulemaking process (public comment, judicial review) that a rule repeal would require.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: EPA disputed the Environmental Integrity Project's methodology/findings without providing its own competing enforcement-count figure in the sourcing reviewed; a single-year figure can be affected by case-timing and referral-pipeline factors, though the reported 76-81% declines relative to comparable first-year baselines suggest more than ordinary year-to-year variance. The civil-enforcement-funding percentage and its underlying dollar figures (30% cut, $201.3M to $61.1M) as reported in secondary coverage do not arithmetically reconcile -- treat the percentage as the reported headline figure and verify the underlying dollar amounts against the Environmental Integrity Project's report directly before citing them specifically. The 12%-enforcement-rate figure is specific to air-pollution violations, not water -- no equivalent water-specific enforcement-rate percentage was found in the reporting reviewed, though the 3,001-facility Clean Water Act noncompliance count is water-specific and independently reported.

rule_name: Copper Rule (EPA emissions standards for primary copper smelters, finalized May 13, 2024 under Clean Air Act Section 112)
agency: EPA / White House (Clean Air Act Section 112(i)(4) presidential exemption authority)
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- two-year compliance exemption, not a rule rescission
date_of_action: 2025-10-24 (proclamation reported; White House fact sheet same period)
original_rule_summary: EPA finalized the Copper Rule on May 13, 2024 under Clean Air Act Section 112, imposing stricter emissions limits on the only two primary copper smelters operating in the U.S. -- Freeport-McMoRan's Miami, Arizona smelter and Rio Tinto's Utah smelter -- covering toxic air pollutants including lead, arsenic, mercury, benzene, and dioxins.
what_changed: President Trump issued a proclamation under Clean Air Act Section 112(i)(4) -- a rarely-used provision letting the President exempt a stationary source from a Section 112 standard for up to two years if compliance technology is unavailable and exemption serves the national security interest -- granting Freeport-McMoRan's Arizona smelter a two-year exemption from the Copper Rule's compliance deadlines. The proclamation stated 'the technology to implement the Copper Rule is not available' in a 'commercially viable form' to meet the rule's deadlines, and that preserving domestic smelting capacity was essential to critical-minerals access in a crisis; the accompanying White House fact sheet said imposing the requirements on 'such a limited and already strained domestic industry risks accelerating further closures.' Freeport-McMoRan said the exemption 'provides needed time to assess and plan for appropriate regulatory reconsideration of the Copper Rule.' Rio Tinto's Utah smelter was not affected, as the company had already invested in emissions-capture equipment to comply. This is the same Section 112(i)(4) mechanism -- and, per ProPublica reporting, the same email-based exemption-request process EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin invited industry to use -- already documented in this tracker's epa-ethylene-oxide-sterilizer-emissions-rollback-2026.json entry, where it was applied to exempt 40 sterilization facilities (roughly 45% of that industry) from a different Section 112 rule; this is a second, independently-documented industry where the same national-security exemption authority was invoked to delay compliance with toxic-emissions standards.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump, President
primary_proponent.note: Personally issued the proclamation invoking Section 112(i)(4) exemption authority; the White House's own fact sheet frames the rationale in national-security/domestic-industrial-base terms.

corporate_beneficiaries: Freeport-McMoRan, Inc. -- the only smelter actually granted the exemption (Rio Tinto's Utah facility was not affected, having already achieved compliance)

estimated_health_impact.summary: Delays, for up to two years, tighter limits on toxic air pollutants (lead, arsenic, mercury, benzene, dioxins) from one of only two primary copper smelters operating in the U.S., near the smelter's surrounding Arizona community.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No source reviewed provided a quantified health-impact or cost-savings estimate specific to this exemption (e.g. tons of pollutant delayed, dollar compliance-cost savings, or a mortality/illness estimate) -- the 2024 rule's own cost-benefit analysis, if it exists, was not located in sourcing for this entry; recheck for EPA's or an independent group's quantified estimate of this specific exemption's impact.

confidence_note: The proclamation's existence, legal mechanism, date, and the Freeport/Rio Tinto distinction are well-corroborated across multiple outlets (Reuters via Investing.com/Yahoo/AOL mirrors, Mining Engineering Online, Law.com, the White House's own fact sheet). No quantified health or cost-savings figure specific to this exemption was found -- this entry documents the regulatory action and its stated rationale, not a quantified impact, and should be rechecked if a figure surfaces later.

rule_name: Ethylene Oxide Emissions Standards for Sterilization Facilities (NESHAP Residual Risk and Technology Review)
status: Delayed/Paused (2-year compliance exemption for 40 facilities, ~45% of the industry, proclaimed July 17, 2025) + Proposed Repeal (broader rescission proposed March 17, 2026, not yet finalized; both actions face litigation)
date_of_action: 2025-07-17 (proclamation exempting 40 facilities, ~45% of industry, for two years); 2026-03-17 (broader repeal proposed) -- comment period on the broader proposal subsequently extended to 2026-05
original_rule_summary: A 2024 EPA rule tightened emissions standards for ethylene oxide (EtO) -- a chemical used to sterilize medical equipment and classified as a potent human carcinogen -- at commercial sterilization facilities nationwide. EPA projected the rule would cut annual EtO emissions from these facilities by roughly 90% by 2027, and it required larger sterilizers (those using at least 10 tons of EtO per year) to install stronger emissions-control technology and implement continuous monitoring.
what_changed: On March 17, 2026, EPA proposed rescinding significant portions of the 2024 EtO rule. The proposal argues EPA overstepped its legal authority under Clean Air Act Section 112(f)(2) when it performed a new residual-risk review as part of the 2024 rulemaking, and on that basis would rescind the tighter risk-based emissions standards the 2024 rule imposed. The proposal would additionally relax technology-based emissions standards specifically for facilities using at least 10 tons of EtO per year and rescind the requirement that larger chemical sterilizers implement continuous emissions monitoring. AP reported the change would affect dozens of sterilization facilities across the country. EPA extended the public comment period on the proposal into May 2026. Separately -- and preceding the March 2026 proposed rescission -- President Trump signed Proclamation 10959 on July 17, 2025 (published in the Federal Register July 23, 2025), invoking Clean Air Act Section 112(i)(4) national-security authority to exempt 40 sterilization facilities, roughly 45% of the industry, from the 2024 rule's compliance deadlines for two years. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin had invited companies to email the agency directly to request exemptions. The Southern Environmental Law Center and NRDC, representing environmental groups in North Carolina, Georgia, and Virginia, sued Trump, EPA, and Zeldin in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (filed late January 2026, per MedTech Dive reporting), arguing the Clean Air Act permits this kind of exemption only when compliance technology is unavailable or genuine national-security interests are at stake -- not as a general deregulatory tool. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0670): the same Section 112(i)(4) national-security exemption authority was separately invoked on Freeport-McMoRan's Arizona copper smelter in October 2025, tracked in its own entry (epa-copper-smelter-emissions-exemption-2025.json) -- a second, independently-documented industry where this mechanism delayed toxic-emissions compliance.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: Directly tied to the July 2025 exemption action: Zeldin invited companies to email EPA requesting exemptions from the 2024 rule, which fed into the July 17, 2025 presidential proclamation exempting ~45% of the industry. Sourcing reviewed did not separately identify a specific named official driving the March 2026 proposed rescission beyond the agency's own legal-authority rationale in that proposed rule -- the two actions are distinct and this note attributes each accordingly.

corporate_beneficiaries: Commercial sterilization facility operators subject to the 2024 rule's technology and monitoring requirements (not further individually named in sourcing reviewed)

estimated_health_impact.summary: Ethylene oxide is a potent human carcinogen; scientists link long-term exposure to elevated risk of leukemia, breast cancer, and lymphoma. Rolling back the 2024 rule's ~90% projected emissions reduction would leave workers at and communities near the affected sterilization facilities exposed to higher EtO levels than the 2024 rule intended to achieve by 2027 -- AP reported many of these communities are already disproportionately low-income and minority neighborhoods near industrial sterilization sites.

rule_name: Fenceline air-monitoring and emissions-reporting reform for coke ovens, chemical plants, and other high-risk industrial sources (multiple NESHAP rules requiring real monitors in place of industry self-estimated 'emission factors')
status: Trump granted U.S. Steel's Clairton Coke Works and other coking plants a two-year exemption from fenceline benzene-monitoring requirements; EPA separately halted planned permanent-monitor requirements at 130+ industrial plants nationwide and granted two-year exemptions to roughly 50 chemical plants, while beginning formal 'reconsideration' of three underlying fenceline-monitoring rules. No reversal of these actions had been identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry.
date_of_action: 2025 (exemptions and rule-reconsideration begin following Trump's January 2025 inauguration) through 2025-11-04 (ProPublica's investigation published)
original_rule_summary: For decades, EPA allowed industrial facilities -- including coke ovens, chemical plants, and other high-risk sources -- to estimate their own air-toxics emissions using standardized 'emission factors' rather than direct measurement, despite EPA itself acknowledging since 1990 that many of these factors, particularly for coke ovens, were 'poor' or 'below average' in accuracy. Biden-era NESHAP rules moved toward requiring real fenceline (perimeter) air monitors at the highest-risk facility types specifically to replace this self-reported 'honor system' with actual measured data and to trigger corrective action when measured concentrations exceeded action levels.
what_changed: A ProPublica investigation published November 4, 2025 found that when EPA required 20 industrial facilities to install temporary fenceline monitors in 2023, actual measured emissions exceeded company self-reported estimates in 97% of cases, often dramatically: benzene at U.S. Steel's Clairton Coke Works (Pittsburgh) measured 37 times higher than estimated; vinyl chloride at a Dow Chemical plant in Plaquemine, Louisiana measured 156 times higher, with ethylene dichloride at the same facility measuring 1,033 times higher; ethylene dichloride at a Formosa plant in Point Comfort, Texas measured 69 times higher; and ethylene oxide at an Indorama plant in Port Neches, Texas measured 7 times the EPA's own new standard. Following Trump's inauguration, EPA halted requirements for permanent fenceline monitors at more than 130 industrial plants nationwide, granted two-year compliance exemptions to roughly 50 chemical plants, and began formally 'reconsidering' three of the underlying fenceline-monitoring rules. U.S. Steel separately applied for its own exemption for the Clairton plant -- obtained by ProPublica via public-records request -- arguing the fenceline benzene-monitoring requirement was too stringent given 'many miles of piping and thousands of valves and flanges at a coke facility' that would be costly and complex to fully seal. President Trump subsequently granted Clairton and other coking plants nationwide a two-year exemption from the fenceline benzene-monitoring requirement specifically. EPA's own modeling found the new monitoring-triggered standards would have reduced the number of people facing unacceptable cancer risk near larger chemical plants from roughly 90,000 to roughly 3,000, a 97% reduction -- a reduction now delayed or at risk depending on the rules' ultimate 'reconsideration' outcome.

rule_name: EPA's Proposed Elimination of the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP)
status: Proposed Repeal (not yet finalized -- EPA extended the 2025 reporting deadline separately to October 30, 2026, and said it would finalize the broader elimination in one or more later actions)
original_rule_summary: The Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, established in 2009, has required roughly 8,000 large industrial facilities -- power plants, refineries, landfills, and other major emitters -- to measure and publicly report their greenhouse gas emissions to EPA annually, producing the U.S. government's primary facility-level emissions dataset used by regulators, researchers, states, and industry itself.
what_changed: On September 12, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin proposed effectively ending the GHGRP, removing reporting obligations for all source categories except petroleum and natural gas systems (those facilities would still report starting in 2034, tied to the separate methane emissions tax). EPA framed the proposal as cutting 'burdensome, costly' red tape, estimating it would save regulated companies up to $2.4 billion. The proposal drew unusually bipartisan pushback: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and Kevin Cramer (R-ND) jointly urged EPA to withdraw it, warning that ending the program would harm American industrial competitiveness and specifically damage the domestic carbon-capture and LNG sectors, which rely on GHGRP data to verify emissions for federal tax credits (the Section 45Q carbon-sequestration credit and Section 45V clean-hydrogen credit). Rep. Sean Casten (D-IL) led a separate House Democratic letter arguing the elimination violated 'clear congressional directives.' EPA received more than 50,000 public comments by the November 3, 2025 deadline. As of early 2026, EPA had not finalized the core elimination; instead it finalized a narrower action extending the 2025 reporting-year deadline to October 30, 2026, stating it would address the rest of the reconsideration proposal in later, separate final actions.

primary_proponent.note: Announced the proposed elimination September 12, 2025, framing it as cost-saving deregulation; the proposal was part of the same broader deregulatory push launched by his March 12, 2025 announcement of 31 simultaneous rollback actions.

corporate_beneficiaries: Large industrial emitters relieved of annual GHG reporting obligations, per EPA's own $2.4 billion cost-savings estimate

estimated_health_impact.summary: Eliminating mandatory facility-level emissions reporting would not itself change physical emissions, but would remove the primary public dataset regulators, researchers, downstream industries (carbon capture, clean hydrogen), and communities use to track where large sources of greenhouse gas pollution are located and how they change over time.

rule_name: Methane emission rules for low-producing ('stripper') oil and gas wells
status: Proposed Repeal -- rulemaking process underway as of ProPublica's June 2026 reporting
original_rule_summary: In 2024, the Biden administration issued the first-ever federal methane emission regulations targeting low-producing 'stripper' wells -- older wells that individually produce little oil or gas but, in aggregate, emit outsized quantities of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, relative to their energy output.
what_changed: The Trump EPA is engineering a rollback of the 2024 stripper-well methane rules. ProPublica reported the rulemaking effort is being led in significant part by Aaron Szabo, a former lobbyist for Hilcorp -- a privately held oil and gas company owned by Texas billionaire Jeffery Hildebrand -- whom Trump named to a top EPA post. Hilcorp specializes in buying up old, low-producing stripper wells and is one of the industry's largest methane emitters relative to its output. Hildebrand and his wife have donated more than $15 million to Trump and other Republican federal candidates since 2020, giving substantially more after the 2024 methane rule was issued. Separately, per the same June 2026 Source New Mexico reporting, Republican lawmakers have introduced legislation that would permanently exempt stripper wells from EPA methane regulation entirely -- a legislative track running alongside the administrative rollback effort.

primary_proponent.note: Named by ProPublica as leading the rulemaking effort to unravel the stripper-well methane rules, working with industry trade groups backed by Hildebrand -- the same rules his former client, Hilcorp, is a primary beneficiary of repealing.

corporate_beneficiaries: Hilcorp (Jeffery Hildebrand, owner) -- specializes in low-producing stripper wells and is one of the industry's largest methane emitters relative to output

rule_name: EPA's Fast-Tracked Approval of New PFAS ('Forever Chemical') Pesticides
status: Finalized (multiple approvals; additional PFAS pesticides reported pending)
date_of_action: 2025-11 (cyclobutrifluram and isocycloseram approved) through 2025-12 (broader reporting on the fast-tracked approval pattern)
original_rule_summary: EPA pesticide registration under FIFRA requires the agency to find that a new pesticide will not cause 'unreasonable adverse effects' on human health or the environment before approving it for use; PFAS-class pesticides -- built around carbon-fluorine bonds that make them extremely persistent and difficult to break down -- had previously been approved at a markedly slower pace.
what_changed: In early November 2025, EPA approved cyclobutrifluram, a fungicide for use on golf courses, lawns, cotton, soybeans, and lettuce, and known to break down into trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), described by researchers as one of the most pervasive PFAS water contaminants in the world. Roughly two weeks later, EPA approved isocycloseram, an insecticide for golf courses, lawns, and food crops including oranges, tomatoes, almonds, peas, and oats; among the health concerns cited by EWG and other reviewers were reduced testicle size, lower sperm count, and liver toxicity in animal studies. Public-health and environmental groups (EWG, the Center for Biological Diversity) characterized both as part of a broader acceleration: in less than two years, EPA authorized five PFAS pesticides -- roughly quintupling the pace of the prior administration, which approved just one PFAS pesticide across four years. EPA and some agricultural-industry commentators pushed back on aspects of the PFAS characterization itself, with AGDAILY arguing environmental groups had 'stretched' the PFAS classification for some of the newly registered products.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: EPA's Office of Pesticide Programs, under Zeldin's leadership, approved both pesticides via the standard registration process; no source reviewed identified an individual official personally directing the accelerated pace beyond the administration's general deregulatory posture.

corporate_beneficiaries: Pesticide manufacturers of cyclobutrifluram and isocycloseram, and agricultural users of both products (named manufacturers not identified in sourcing reviewed)

rule_name: Risk Management Program 'Common Sense Approach' Rollback
agency: EPA (Office of Land and Emergency Management)
status: Proposed (comment period closed May 11, 2026; EPA has stated intent to finalize in late 2026)
original_rule_summary: The 2024 Safer Communities by Chemical Accident Prevention (SCCAP) rule, finalized under the Biden EPA, strengthened Risk Management Program (RMP) requirements under Clean Air Act Section 112(r) for roughly 11,700-11,900 facilities handling extremely hazardous substances. Key provisions included mandatory Safer Technology and Alternatives Analyses (STAA) with implementation requirements for high-accident-rate sectors (chemical manufacturing, petroleum/coal products), third-party compliance audits, expanded public disclosure of chemical hazard information, natural-hazard and power-loss risk assessment requirements, worker protections including anonymous hazard reporting and stop-work authority, and enhanced community/emergency-responder notification systems.
what_changed: On February 24, 2026, EPA published a proposed rule, the 'Common Sense Approach to Chemical Accident Prevention,' that would rescind or substantially scale back most of the 2024 SCCAP requirements. Key rollbacks: eliminating STAA requirements for existing facilities in the two highest-risk sectors (chemical manufacturing and petroleum/coal products, NAICS 324/325), limiting STAA to newly built processes only; rescinding most third-party audit requirements (with a narrower option requiring audits only for facilities with 2+ accidents in 5 years); eliminating the requirement to share chemical hazard information directly with the public on request, relying instead on EPA's more limited online Data Tool; and rescinding several worker-protection provisions including anonymous reporting, stop-work authority, and mandatory workers' rights training. EPA frames the changes as realigning RMP with OSHA's existing Process Safety Management standard and removing 'duplicative' requirements. The proposal followed a March 2025 EPA announcement that it would reconsider the SCCAP rule, itself prompted by Executive Orders 14148 and 14154 directing agencies to rescind Biden-era regulatory actions. The public comment period closed May 11, 2026; as of this writing the rule remains a proposal, with EPA's own regulatory agenda indicating a target of finalizing it in late 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.note: Announced on March 12, 2025 that EPA would reconsider the 2024 SCCAP rule; EPA under his leadership published the Common Sense Approach proposed rule in February 2026 and held the required public hearing in March 2026.

corporate_beneficiaries: Roughly 11,700-11,900 RMP-regulated facilities nationwide, concentrated in chemical manufacturing and petroleum/coal products refining -- sectors represented in commenting by the American Chemistry Council, American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, American Petroleum Institute, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, all of which had petitioned against the 2024 rule before this rollback was proposed.

EPA's own estimated population near RMP facilities is disproportionately exposed to accident risk.

rule_name: EPA's Attempt to Vacate the 2024 Soot (PM2.5) Air Quality Standard
status: Rejected by federal appeals court -- the 2024 standard remains in effect

rule_name: Procedures for Chemical Risk Evaluation Under TSCA (2025 Framework Rule proposal)
agency: EPA (Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention)
status: Proposed (comment period closed November 7, 2025; EPA's regulatory agenda has targeted a final rule for mid-2026)
original_rule_summary: The 2024 TSCA Risk Evaluation Framework Rule, finalized under the Biden EPA, required the agency to evaluate all conditions of use of a chemical and all exposure pathways (not a subset chosen by EPA) when determining whether it poses an "unreasonable risk" under Section 6 of the Toxic Substances Control Act, and barred EPA from assuming workers use personal protective equipment (PPE) correctly when estimating occupational exposure -- on the reasoning that assuming correct PPE use could understate real-world risk to workers. It also required a single, whole-chemical risk determination rather than separate determinations per condition of use.
what_changed: On September 23, 2025, EPA published a proposed rule amending the TSCA Risk Evaluation Framework for the third time since 2017 ("Take 3"). The proposal would reinstate an assumption that workers handling toxic chemicals use correct PPE and follow applicable engineering/administrative controls when EPA estimates occupational exposure -- reversing the 2024 rule's bar on that assumption. It would also require EPA to issue a separate unreasonable-risk determination for each condition of use of a chemical rather than one determination for the chemical as a whole, and would scale back manufacturer information-request obligations to what is "known to or reasonably ascertainable," reducing data requirements the 2024 rule had expanded. The public comment period closed November 7, 2025; EPA's own regulatory agenda has targeted finalizing the rule by mid-2026, though the exact date has been reported inconsistently (April vs. July 2026) across legal-industry trackers.

rule_name: Elimination of the Endangered Species Act's "blanket" Section 4(d) rule, plus a new economic/national-security exclusion for critical habitat designations under Section 4(b)(2)
agency: Department of the Interior (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service) and Department of Commerce (NOAA/NMFS)
status: Finalized -- announced July 17, 2026; published in the Federal Register; effective August 20, 2026 (blanket-rule change applies prospectively only, to species newly listed or reclassified as threatened after that date, not to species already listed as threatened)
original_rule_summary: Since the 1970s, FWS's 'blanket' Section 4(d) rule automatically extended the same protections against killing, harassment, and harm that endangered species receive to any species newly listed or reclassified as 'threatened' (the less-imperiled of the ESA's two protected categories), while the agency worked out a tailored, species-specific rule. Separately, Section 4(b)(2) previously allowed only limited consideration of economic impact when the agency designated a species' 'critical habitat.'
what_changed: On November 20, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, FWS, and NOAA/NMFS jointly proposed eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule and revising the critical-habitat-exclusion standard under Section 4(b)(2) to allow agencies to weigh economic impact and national security more heavily when deciding whether to exclude land from a critical habitat designation. The package was finalized July 17, 2026. Under the new regime, newly listed or reclassified threatened species no longer receive automatic protection against killing or harm the moment they are listed -- FWS must instead draft an individual, species-specific 4(d) rule for each one, a process advocacy groups warn is 'far more time-consuming and resource-intensive' and will create gaps in protection while individual rules are drafted. The change applies prospectively only, to species listed or reclassified after August 20, 2026; it does not strip protections already in place for currently-listed threatened species. FWS Director Brian Nesvik framed the change as enabling 'a more cooperative relationship with the American people'; Burgum said the ESA had been 'weaponized to stop almost any new project in America, driving up costs for families, weakening our competitiveness, and undermining our national security,' and separately that nearly 97% of species ever listed under the ESA remain listed today, citing that as evidence the law has not succeeded at its stated recovery goal. The same November 20, 2025 announcement also proposed the separate rescission of the ESA's habitat-modification 'harm' definition, documented in the companion entry [[esa-harm-definition-rollback-2026]] -- that rule followed its own, earlier timeline (proposed April 2025, finalized July 11, 2026) and rests on a different statutory provision (the definition of 'take'/'harm' under Sections 3 and 9), but both actions were promoted together as one package and finalized within days of each other in July 2026. Named species cited by reporting as illustrative of what is at stake under a weakened listing regime include the monarch butterfly, Florida manatee, California spotted owl, North American wolverine, and Yarrow's spiny lizard (for which a separate listing petition was filed the same week as the November 2025 announcement). The Property and Environment Research Center and Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation had already sued Interior in March 2026 arguing the (then-still-proposed) blanket rule was illegal on separate, pro-deregulation grounds (that FWS lacked authority to have created the blanket rule in the first place); Earthjustice, Humane World for Animals, and Humane World Action Fund oppose the rollback, with Humane World Action Fund president Sara Amundson calling the decision 'a profound failure by Interior Secretary Burgum and his department.'

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.note: Announced and finalized the change jointly with FWS Director Brian Nesvik and NOAA/NMFS; publicly framed the ESA as 'weaponized' against development and cited the 97%-not-delisted figure as justification.

corporate_beneficiaries: Logging, mining, oil and gas, and other development interests seeking faster permitting for projects affecting newly threatened-listed species' habitat

estimated_health_impact.summary: This is an ecological/species-conservation rollback rather than a direct human-health standard. The concrete risk critics identify is a protection gap for newly listed threatened species during the time FWS takes to draft individual species-specific rules -- previously bridged automatically by the blanket rule -- with named species (monarch butterfly, Florida manatee, California spotted owl, North American wolverine, Yarrow's spiny lizard) cited as illustrative of what could be affected by future listings. No sourcing reviewed provided a quantified extinction-risk or species-count estimate specific to this rule change.

rule_name: Rescission of the Endangered Species Act's regulatory definition of "harm" to include habitat destruction (50 C.F.R. § 17.3)
agency: Department of the Interior (Fish and Wildlife Service) and Department of Commerce (NOAA/NMFS)
status: Finalized -- rule uploaded to the Federal Register July 2026, effective September 14, 2026; multiple lawsuits filed or noticed
original_rule_summary: Since 1975 (revised 1981), federal regulations defined 'harm' to a protected species under the Endangered Species Act to include 'significant habitat modification or degradation where it actually kills or injures wildlife by significantly impairing essential behavioral patterns, including breeding, feeding, or sheltering.' This definition meant that destroying or significantly degrading a species' critical habitat -- not just directly killing or injuring an individual animal -- could itself violate the ESA's prohibition on 'take' of a listed species, and was the legal basis on which courts and agencies had evaluated development, logging, mining, and drilling proposals in critical habitat for nearly five decades.
what_changed: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0245): the rescission finalized in July 2026 was first proposed over a year earlier. On April 17, 2025, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service jointly proposed rescinding the same 'harm' definition, drawing more than 242,000 public comments during a comment period that closed May 19, 2025. At the time, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said 'President Trump is rescinding overly broad and burdensome regulations that have restrained our fishermen for too long,' and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the administration was restoring the ESA 'to its original intent' while respecting the livelihoods of Americans who depend on the land. On July 11, 2026, the Departments of the Interior and Commerce announced they were rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm' that had included significant habitat modification or degradation, eliminating that language entirely from the operative regulation. The rule was uploaded to the Federal Register and takes effect September 14, 2026. Under the new, narrower definition, development activities that destroy or degrade a protected species' habitat would no longer, on their own, constitute unlawful 'harm' to that species -- only actions that directly kill or injure individual animals would qualify. The Center for Biological Diversity, Sierra Club, and Conservation Law Foundation immediately filed suit, arguing the rescission 'violates the core purpose of the statute and decades of legal precedent'; Defenders of Wildlife separately sent a notice of intent to sue, arguing that 'destroying the habitat of endangered wildlife harms that species.'

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.note: Interior, jointly with the Department of Commerce, announced and finalized the rescission of the habitat-modification language from the ESA 'harm' definition.

corporate_beneficiaries.connection: Development projects that significantly degrade protected species' habitat -- without directly killing or injuring individual animals -- would no longer require the same level of ESA review or mitigation that the habitat-modification definition had required for nearly 50 years.

rule_name: Rescission of the FCC's Section 105 telecom network-security rule (the 'Salt Typhoon rule')
status: Finalized -- FCC voted to rescind in November 2025
original_rule_summary: In January 2025, in the final days of the Biden administration, the FCC adopted a rule under Section 105 of the Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act (CALEA) requiring telecommunications carriers to affirmatively secure their networks against unauthorized access, in direct response to the Salt Typhoon intrusion -- a China-linked state-sponsored hacking campaign that had infiltrated at least eight major U.S. telecom carriers, geolocating millions of Americans and intercepting call and text data, in one of the largest telecom breaches in U.S. history.
what_changed: On November 20, 2025, the FCC, under Chairman Brendan Carr, voted along party lines to rescind the Section 105 network-security rule adopted less than a year earlier in direct response to Salt Typhoon. Carr argued the rule 'exceeded the agency's authority' and 'did not present an effective or agile response to the relevant cybersecurity threats,' framing it as a rushed, ineffective, last-minute Biden-era action. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA), the Senate Commerce Committee's ranking member, publicly opposed the rollback, sending a formal letter to Carr in November 2025 and noting the reversal came after direct lobbying from the same telecom carriers whose networks had been breached by the Salt Typhoon hackers the rule was written to guard against.

primary_proponent.name: Brendan Carr
primary_proponent.note: Led the party-line vote to rescind the rule, characterizing it as exceeding FCC authority and ineffective, rather than defending it as insufficiently protective against the threat it was written to address.

rule_name: FDA Consumer Warning Webpage Against Chlorine Dioxide and Other Unproven Autism 'Treatments'
status: Fully Repealed (webpage removed, not republished)
date_of_action: 2025-05 (webpage first found removed, per Wired) through late 2025 (HHS's own stated removal timing)
original_rule_summary: FDA maintained a consumer-facing warning page, unchanged since 2019, advising against chlorine dioxide (marketed as 'Miracle Mineral Solution'/MMS), raw camel milk, and other unproven products promoted online as cures or treatments for autism -- part of FDA's ordinary consumer-protection messaging, not a binding regulation, but the agency's clearest public statement that ingesting chlorine dioxide is dangerous and not an approved treatment for anything.
what_changed: By June 2025, Wired reported the FDA's chlorine dioxide/autism-treatments warning page had quietly disappeared from the agency's website, coinciding with a surge in online chlorine dioxide/MMS promotion following remarks HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made about the substance during his confirmation process, and with previously prosecuted or investigated 'bleach cure' promoters re-emerging and connecting with Trump-aligned figures, including at events at Trump's Doral resort. A more thorough investigation by ProPublica, published roughly eight months later, confirmed the page's removal and obtained HHS's own explanation: the department said it had retired the page 'during a routine clean up of dated content at the end of 2025,' framing it as content-maintenance rather than a policy reversal. The page has not been restored or replaced with updated guidance as of the most recent reporting reviewed. Chlorine dioxide/MMS advocates interpreted the removal as a positive signal, with one telling ProPublica they hoped the new administration, with Kennedy at HHS, might now allow chlorine dioxide to be studied as a legitimate therapeutic.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services (FDA's parent department)

Kennedy is included as the department's accountable head and because his own public chlorine-dioxide-adjacent remarks during confirmation are documented by Wired as contemporaneous context for the surge in advocacy the removal coincided with -- see confidence_note for this attribution's limits.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Chlorine dioxide/MMS ingestion has documented, FDA-recorded harms including severe vomiting, severe diarrhea, life-threatening dehydration-induced low blood pressure, acute liver failure, and death; removing FDA's own consumer warning removes a specific, checkable public deterrent against a product with a known toxicity record, at a moment reporting found renewed promotional activity around it.

rule_name: FDA Marketing Restriction on Ingestible Fluoride Supplement Products for Children
status: Finalized (marketing-restriction action taken; FDA stopped short of a formal product ban)
date_of_action: 2025-03-10 (Utah becomes first state to ban water fluoridation, RFK Jr. publicly signals a coordinated federal push) through 2025-10-31 (FDA announces fluoride-supplement marketing restriction)
original_rule_summary: Ingestible fluoride supplements (drops and tablets) have been available, without a formal FDA approval process, as a decades-old preventive dental-health option recommended by dentists and pediatricians for children -- particularly those under 3 and those at higher cavity risk -- who lack access to fluoridated drinking water, most often in rural areas or private-well communities. The American Dental Association and American Academy of Pediatrics have long supported graduated fluoride supplementation for high-risk children starting at six months of age as safe and effective cavity prevention.
what_changed: As newly installed HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. publicly pushed to eliminate water fluoridation nationwide -- posting that the administration would 'advise all U.S. water systems to remove fluoride from public water' -- Utah's legislature moved first: Republican Gov. Spencer Cox announced on March 10, 2025 that he would sign, and signed by March 28, 2025, a law making Utah the first state to ban fluoride from public drinking water systems, over opposition from dentists and the American Dental Association. With water fluoridation itself outside FDA's direct authority, the agency instead targeted the alternative lawmakers and advocates had pointed to for communities without fluoridated water: on October 31, 2025, the FDA announced it was moving to restrict the sale of ingestible fluoride supplement products for children, sending notices to four manufacturers about marketing supplements to children under 3 and to older children with low or moderate cavity risk, along with warning letters to healthcare professionals who prescribe them. The FDA stopped short of an outright ban on the products. Separately, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton opened investigations into Colgate-Palmolive and Procter & Gamble over children's fluoride toothpaste marketing; both companies settled by agreeing to depict pea-sized amounts rather than larger swirls in promotional imagery, while maintaining their products already complied with FDA requirements.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Publicly announced the administration's intent to move against water fluoridation nationally and has repeatedly claimed fluoride causes 'profound IQ loss' and other health harms; the FDA action against ingestible supplements followed under his HHS oversight after the water-fluoridation push itself proved outside FDA's direct regulatory reach.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Fluoride is one of the most effective, low-cost tools for preventing tooth decay, particularly for children without access to fluoridated water. The American Dental Association and American Academy of Pediatrics both opposed the FDA's restriction, warning it removes a supported option for exactly the population -- children in non-fluoridated, often lower-income rural communities -- who benefit most, and that restricting supply will likely raise cavity rates in those areas. The National Institutes of Health has said toxic fluoride overdoses are rare accidents, not a risk from standard supplement or water-fluoridation dosing, cutting against the safety rationale cited for the restriction.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No independently quantified national estimate of cavity-rate increase or dollar cost attributable specifically to this restriction was identified in sourcing reviewed; the harm case here rests on the established dental-health consensus (ADA, AAP, NIH) that fluoride supplementation is a safe, effective, and until now clinically recommended prevention tool being narrowed on disputed scientific grounds, rather than on a modeled figure.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the sequence of events (Utah's law, RFK Jr.'s public statements, the FDA's October 31, 2025 marketing-restriction action, and ADA/AAP opposition), corroborated by CNN, NBC News, STAT News, and ProPublica's detailed reporting on the FDA action and Paxton's parallel toothpaste-marketing investigations. MODERATE confidence on classifying this as a Corporate Deregulation consumer_safety rollback rather than a Government Services Redirection entry -- Utah's own ban is a state action outside this tracker's federal scope and is included here only as context for the coordinated national campaign RFK Jr. publicly announced; the entry's tracked action is anchored specifically to the FDA's federal marketing restriction.
short_summary: FDA restricted marketing of children's fluoride supplements as RFK Jr. pushed to end water fluoridation nationally.

rule_name: FDA's longstanding requirement that new drugs be supported by two independent clinical studies before approval
status: Finalized (policy change announced)
original_rule_summary: FDA has long applied a default expectation that new drug approvals be supported by two independent, adequate, and well-controlled clinical studies -- a standard intended to guard against a single trial's results being a statistical fluke, methodological artifact, or site-specific anomaly, and to provide independent replication of a drug's safety and efficacy findings before it reaches the market.
what_changed: FDA announced it will end its longstanding two-independent-study requirement for new drug approvals, moving to a default standard of a single trial, with the stated goal of accelerating drug approvals. The change was led by FDA Commissioner Marty Makary and vaccine/biologics official Dr. Vinay Prasad -- the same official whose office separately refused to even review Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine application over trial-design objections (see fda-moderna-mrna-flu-vaccine-refusal-2026.json), creating an apparent tension between accelerating approval standards for new drugs generally while applying an unusually strict, refusal-to-file standard in that specific vaccine case. Days later, Commissioner Makary announced a related acceleration measure: a pilot 'Reviewer Recognition and Excellence' program offering quarterly cash bonuses (starting around August 2026) to drug reviewers who complete evaluations ahead of schedule, tied to 'weighted time savings' and work-quality/complexity metrics. Makary told FDA staff the payments were meant to 'recognize and reward staff who find ways to be more efficient,' and that securing approval for the bonuses took 'some wrangling.'

primary_proponent.name: Dr. Marty Makary / Dr. Vinay Prasad
primary_proponent.role: FDA Commissioner / FDA vaccine and biologics official
primary_proponent.note: The administration's stated rationale is accelerating the pace of drug approvals and reducing development costs and timelines for pharmaceutical companies.

corporate_beneficiaries: Pharmaceutical companies seeking faster, lower-cost paths to drug approval, since a single required trial substantially reduces development time and cost compared to two independent studies

estimated_health_impact.summary: Replication across independent studies has historically served as a safeguard against approving drugs based on results that don't hold up under a second trial -- a single-trial default standard increases the risk that approved drugs' safety/efficacy profiles rest on findings that would not have replicated, a tradeoff FDA is making explicitly in favor of faster approval timelines.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: FDA retains discretion to require additional studies for specific drugs under the new default policy; this entry documents the announced change in the default standard, not a claim that every future approval under it will prove unsafe or ineffective.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the policy announcement, its FDA leadership attribution (Makary and Prasad), and its stated acceleration rationale are confirmed by AP's direct reporting, with no dispute of the underlying facts identified in sourcing reviewed.
short_summary: FDA ended its default two-independent-study requirement for new drug approvals, moving to a single-trial standard to accelerate approvals.

rule_name: HUD Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity (FHEO) guidance on assistance animal accommodations under the Fair Housing Act
status: Finalized (guidance permanently rescinded and replaced)
original_rule_summary: HUD's longstanding guidance treated a broad category of 'assistance animals' -- including untrained emotional support animals (ESAs) providing comfort to people with mental health or emotional disabilities -- as presumptively reasonable accommodation requests under the Fair Housing Act, requiring housing providers to accommodate them on largely the same footing as trained service animals, without a training requirement.
what_changed: HUD's FHEO permanently rescinded its longstanding ESA guidance and issued a new enforcement standard realigning federal fair-housing practice closer to the ADA's stricter service-animal framework. Under the new standard, requests involving trained assistance animals remain presumptively reasonable, but requests involving untrained emotional support animals are not -- the operative requirement is now training to perform a disability-related task, not emotional comfort alone (though unlike the ADA, the new HUD standard still permits species other than dogs, provided the animal is trained). The memorandum directs all open ESA cases to be reevaluated under the new, stricter standard. Disability-rights advocates (DREDF) characterized HUD as now 'an enforcement agency that won't enforce' emotional-support-animal accommodation claims it previously treated as presumptively valid.

rule_name: Public-lands oil, gas, and coal extraction rules -- bonding requirements and methane venting/flaring standards
status: Proposed Repeal -- rulemaking announced June 2026
original_rule_summary: Biden-era Interior Department rules required oil and gas companies drilling on public lands to post financial bonds of up to $500,000 to guarantee funds are available to clean up and plug wells after extraction ends, and required companies to detail plans to limit methane emissions -- including restrictions on venting and flaring, both of which release methane, a potent greenhouse gas -- when applying for drilling permits.
what_changed: The Interior Department, under Secretary Doug Burgum, proposed rolling back regulations for oil, gas, and coal extraction on public lands.
