The same rulemaking package separately proposes shrinking public comment periods for oil and gas lease sales from 90 days to 10 days, by eliminating both 30-day scoping and 30-day draft-document comment periods. The proposal's own public comment period remains open through August 24, 2026; no final rule has been published. Re-verified 2026-08-22: the proposal was formally published in the Federal Register on June 24, 2026 as "Oil and Gas Leasing" (BLM-2025-0037, FR doc. 2026-12734), confirming this is now the operative proposed-rule text rather than only a June announcement. rule_name: 5% Cost Safe Harbor for Establishing 'Beginning of Construction' on Wind and Solar Projects (IRC Sections 45Y/48E Clean Electricity Tax Credits)
status: Weakened, then vacated by a federal court -- IRS Notice 2025-42 (Aug. 15, 2025) eliminated the safe harbor; the U.S. District Court for D.D.C. vacated the notice in its entirety on June 6, 2026, finding it arbitrary and capricious, and remanded to the IRS
original_rule_summary: Before this action, developers of wind and most solar projects could establish that construction had 'begun' for purposes of qualifying for the Clean Electricity Production Credit (IRC Section 45Y) and Clean Electricity Investment Credit (IRC Section 48E) either by satisfying a physical-work test or by incurring at least 5% of a project's total cost before a deadline -- the '5% Safe Harbor,' a longstanding IRS administrative rule that let projects lock in credit eligibility years before construction was physically underway, which developers, financiers, and utilities had relied on for planning and financing large-scale projects.
what_changed: On August 15, 2025, Treasury and the IRS issued Notice 2025-42, implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's (signed July 4, 2025) phase-out of wind and solar tax credits pursuant to Executive Order 14315 (July 7, 2025). The notice eliminated the 5% Safe Harbor for wind projects and for solar projects exceeding 1.5 megawatts that had not already established beginning-of-construction status under prior guidance by September 1, 2025 -- leaving the stricter 'physical work of a significant nature' test as the only way such projects could qualify. Industry groups said this would harm projects that had been in planning, design, and financing for months or years while relying on the 5% Safe Harbor's availability. The Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) said political attacks on solar and storage -- including this notice, the broader OBBBA tax-credit phase-out, and other executive/agency actions -- threatened more than 500 planned projects totaling nearly 116 gigawatts, over half of all U.S. power capacity planned to be built through 2030, and could cut previously projected 2025-2030 solar installations (up to 330 GW) by as much as 38%. Industry groups and Democratic lawmakers contrasted this with China, which added more than 430 gigawatts of new wind and solar capacity in 2025 alone -- more than the U.S. and the rest of the world combined in the first half of the year -- arguing the U.S. rollback would cede clean-energy manufacturing and deployment leadership. A coalition led by the Oregon Environmental Council sued, and on June 6, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Oregon Environmental Council v. IRS, No. CV-25-4400) vacated Notice 2025-42 in its entirety, ruling the IRS had acted arbitrarily and capriciously under the Administrative Procedure Act by eliminating the Safe Harbor without adequately addressing extensive industry comments documenting substantial reliance on it, and remanded the matter back to the IRS. The ruling restored the 5% Safe Harbor, at least pending any further IRS action or appeal.

primary_proponent.note: Directed Treasury/IRS to implement OBBBA's wind/solar tax-credit phase-out via Executive Order 14315 (July 7, 2025), the stated basis for Notice 2025-42.

rule_name: Joint-Employer Standard Narrowing (NLRB)
administration: Trump II (2025-present) -- corrected from an earlier draft that misdated this as a First Term action
status: Fully Repealed (2023 rule withdrawn; 2020 standard reinstated)
original_rule_summary: The NLRB's joint-employer standard determines when two companies (e.g. a franchisor and franchisee, or a company and its staffing agency) can both be held liable for labor law violations and both required to bargain collectively with the same workers. A 2023 Biden-era rule broadened the standard to include 'indirect' or 'reserved' (even unexercised) control over terms like wages, work rules, or health and safety -- making it easier to hold parent companies/franchisors jointly liable.
what_changed: The 2023 rule was vacated by a federal court in March 2024 as 'arbitrary and capricious.' The NLRB (with its quorum restored) formally withdrew the 2023 rule and reinstated the narrower 2020 first-Trump-term standard: an entity is now a joint employer only if it 'possesses and exercises substantial direct and immediate control' over essential terms of employment (wages, benefits, hours, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, direction). Indirect or unexercised control no longer counts.

primary_proponent.name: National Labor Relations Board (agency-level action)
primary_proponent.note: No single named Board member or Chairman was clearly identified as the primary individual driver in sourcing found this session -- the NLRB characterized the rulemaking as 'ministerial,' implementing the court's vacatur rather than a new policy choice by named leadership. Flag attribution as agency-level, not individual, until further verified.

corporate_beneficiaries: Franchisors, staffing agencies, and businesses using subcontractors -- explicitly named as beneficiaries in legal analysis of the rule

estimated_health_impact.summary: Minimal direct physical health impact. The harm is corporate accountability: narrowing joint-employer liability limits the ability to hold parent companies/franchisors responsible for labor violations (including workplace safety violations) occurring at a franchisee's or contractor's site, since the parent company is less likely to be considered a joint employer absent direct, exercised control.
estimated_health_impact.caveat: No quantified health/safety figure exists for this rule -- it is a liability-allocation rule, not a safety standard itself. The health-relevant argument is indirect: reduced accountability for the entity best positioned to enforce safety standards across a franchise/contractor network.

confidence_note: Solid on the facts and timeline (Federal Register citation, clear before/after standard). Two things to flag: (1) this is a Trump II action from Feb. 2026, not Trump I as an earlier version of this tracker listed -- the 2020 rule referenced here was Trump I, but the specific rollback being tracked (reversing the 2023 expansion) happened this year; (2) no individual proponent is clearly named in sourcing, unlike most other entries in this tracker. Update: 2026-09-06 recheck sweep surfaced NLRB General Counsel Crystal Carey's August 2026 Memorandum GC 26-04 -- verified its 13 targeted precedents (severance agreements, captive-audience meetings, bargaining orders, remedies, dues checkoff, etc.) do not include the joint-employer standard. No development found specific to this entry's own tracked rule.

status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- repeated emergency orders overrode planned retirement; legal challenges ongoing

rule_name: MSHA silica exposure rule reconsideration/pause and NIOSH functional elimination
agency: Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) / National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), Dept. of Labor and HHS respectively
status: Indefinitely stayed pending judicial review (8th Circuit stay, originally granted April 11, 2025, formally extended to the MNM conforming amendments via an April 6, 2026 Federal Register notice; the litigation abeyance itself was further extended by at least two more months on August 10, 2026) -- a stronger, clearer status than 'delayed/paused, escalating toward reconsideration,' since the entire rule including the MNM compliance deadline is now confirmed covered by the same court-ordered stay, and the abeyance period MSHA and industry petitioners are using to negotiate has now been running, with court approval, for over a year; Weakened to point of functional elimination (NIOSH)
date_of_action: 2025-04-08 (initial enforcement pause); litigation and reconsideration process ongoing as of mid-2025 through at least Oct 2025
original_rule_summary: A new MSHA silica exposure rule (finalized April 18, 2024 under the Biden administration; effective June 17, 2024) would halve the allowable exposure limit to respirable crystalline silica dust (to 50 micrograms/cubic meter) for coal and metal/nonmetal (MNM) miners, requiring enhanced monitoring, medical surveillance, and respiratory protection, targeting silicosis, black lung disease, and other respiratory illness. Separately, NIOSH is the federal agency that conducts the injury/fatality research and certifies respiratory protection equipment underlying OSHA and MSHA rulemaking.
what_changed: MSHA announced an enforcement pause for coal mine operators on April 8, 2025 (initially through Aug 18, 2025), citing 'unforeseen NIOSH restructuring' affecting the supply of certified respirators and dust monitors. Separately and significantly, the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted industry groups (National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association; National Mining Association) a temporary stay of the rule on April 4, 2025, before MSHA's own pause was announced. By around October 2025, MSHA announced it would 'engage in limited rulemaking to reconsider' portions of the rule under ongoing litigation -- a materially stronger action than an administrative enforcement pause, since it signals MSHA intends to substantively rewrite parts of the rule, not just delay its start date. The metal/nonmetal (MNM) compliance deadline of April 8, 2026 has now passed as of this entry's last verification; this entry's sourcing does not confirm whether that deadline was met, further paused, or is itself subject to the same reconsideration process -- flag for follow-up. Separately, the administration's restructuring eliminated significant NIOSH research capacity (reported layoffs of 870+ NIOSH employees) and closed 11 OSHA field offices in states with the highest workplace fatality rates, plus 34 MSHA offices. Update: this entry previously flagged the passed April 8, 2026 MNM compliance deadline as needing follow-up. That's now resolved -- on April 6, 2026, MSHA published a Federal Register notice formally delaying the effective date of the MNM conforming amendments, confirming the deadline is covered by the same 8th Circuit stay (originally granted April 11, 2025) that paused the coal-sector provisions, rather than having separately taken effect or lapsed unaddressed. MSHA continues enforcing the pre-2024-rule standards in the interim and states it will publish a further Federal Register notice once the judicial stay is terminated. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change to the rule's status -- the 8th Circuit has granted the parties' request to hold the litigation in abeyance while they attempt to resolve the challenge through negotiation, rather than proceeding to a ruling; MSHA reiterated its intent to pursue limited reconsideration rulemaking in a January 2026 status update to the court, consistent with what this entry already documents. Re-verified 2026-08-22: on August 10, 2026, the 8th Circuit granted MSHA's request to extend the litigation abeyance by at least another two months, per West Virginia Gazette-Mail reporting -- MSHA itself asked the court to keep the rule in legal limbo rather than the industry petitioners driving this extension, continuing the negotiated-resolution posture already documented rather than moving toward a ruling or a reconsideration proposal.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Labor leadership under the Trump II administration
primary_proponent.role: MSHA and OSHA are both housed under DOL
primary_proponent.note: Reporting on the specific individual driving the NIOSH cuts ties them to the administration's broader federal workforce restructuring effort (DOGE-linked); a single named proponent for this specific action was not clearly identified in available sourcing -- flag as lower-confidence on attribution and verify before using in debate. The litigation itself was initiated by industry petitioners (NSSGA, National Mining Association), not the administration, though MSHA's subsequent reconsideration rulemaking is an administration action responding to that litigation.

corporate_beneficiaries: Coal and metal/nonmetal mining operators subject to the paused/reconsidered stricter silica exposure limit
National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association and National Mining Association member companies specifically, as the litigants who obtained the initial stay

estimated_health_impact.summary: The Department of Labor's own prior estimate for the silica rule (before the pause/reconsideration) projected substantial prevented deaths and illness -- pausing enforcement and reconsidering the rule puts those prevented cases at risk. Notably, a bipartisan-leaning congressional signal exists on the other side: the Senate Appropriations Committee approved report language (July 31, 2025) directing MSHA to 'fully and effectively enforce' the rule and not use funds to weaken it -- worth citing as a counterpoint showing this is contested even within Congress, not a uniformly one-sided rollback. This is no longer purely a modeled/projected risk: black lung clinics across Appalachia report a real, observed surge in cases, including younger miners (in their 30s and 40s) developing severe and often fatal forms of the disease, driven in part by deeper mining through silica-rich rock as easily accessible coal seams are depleted -- a materializing harm alongside DOL's original prevented-case estimate, not a replacement for it. As of November 2025, AP reported NIOSH's own screening data (11,500 central Appalachian miners' X-rays, mid-2020 through mid-2025) showing 55% of screened miners with some form of black lung and a 62% rate among those screened in just the most recent year -- while NIOSH's own screening and mobile-testing staff were themselves being cut and partially reinstated during the same period documented below, and MSHA's silica-rule enforcement remained paused.

Primary proponent attribution remains unresolved -- no current MSHA leadership was named in this or prior searches as personally driving the agency's position; continue flagging this as the entry's weak point rather than treating it as settled. Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- the 8th Circuit abeyance (extended at least two more months on August 10, 2026) remains in effect; no ruling or new reconsideration proposal identified. rule_name: PFAS ('Forever Chemical') Restrictions on Military Firefighting Foam and Base Cleanup, FY2026 NDAA
status: Weakened (not fully repealed) -- mixed final outcome, distinct from the original committee-stage rollback
date_of_action: 2025-08 (committee-stage provisions first reported) through 2025-12-18 (President Trump signed the final FY2026 NDAA, P.L. 119-60)
original_rule_summary: A 2020-2023 statutory framework (building on earlier NDAAs) required DOD to stop purchasing PFAS-based aqueous film-forming firefighting foam (AFFF) by October 2023 and stop using it by October 2024, paused open burning/incineration of PFAS-contaminated foam and waste pending safer disposal methods, and restricted DOD's purchase of everyday PFAS-treated products (cookware, carpets, etc.).
what_changed: Committee-stage House and Senate FY2026 NDAA text (reported August-September 2025 by the Guardian, The Hill, and Environmental Working Group) would have delayed the firefighting-foam phaseout, repealed the incineration/open-burning pause, rescinded the everyday-PFAS-product purchase restrictions, and cut PFAS-site cleanup funding versus FY2024 levels. The final, enacted NDAA (signed December 18, 2025) is a mixed outcome, not a straight rollback as first reported: it extends DOD's authority to purchase PFAS-based firefighting foam through 2026 and use existing stockpiles through 2028 (rather than the 2023/2024 phaseout deadlines), and grants DOD authority to destroy PFAS waste using 'innovative technologies' approved by federal or state regulators -- softer than the committee-stage full repeal of the incineration pause, but still a loosening of the prior blanket moratorium. The final bill did NOT add new restrictions on PFAS-treated firefighter turnout gear, a gap several outlets flagged as a missed opportunity. Separately, and cutting the other direction, the final NDAA also created a new, first-ever high-level DOD Coordinator position dedicated to PFAS-impacted defense communities, which Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA), who pushed the provision, called 'the strongest federal reform yet for PFAS-impacted defense communities.' Independent of the NDAA itself, Senate Democrats separately pressed the Pentagon in November 2025 over an administrative decision to delay some PFAS site cleanups.

primary_proponent.name: Roger Wicker
primary_proponent.note: Senate Armed Services Committee text carried the most aggressive PFAS rollback provisions (including full repeal of the incineration/open-burning pause, later softened in the final conference outcome); House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers (R-AL) also a central figure in the joint bill's development.

corporate_beneficiaries: PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam manufacturers and defense contractors reliant on existing PFAS-based foam stockpiles
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce publicly lobbied to retain the rollback provisions in the NDAA text

estimated_health_impact.summary: PFAS ('forever chemicals') from firefighting foam have contaminated drinking water and groundwater at hundreds of military installations, with exposure linked to certain cancers, thyroid disruption, immune effects, and other health harms. The rollback provisions extend the window in which DOD may keep purchasing and using PFAS-based foam rather than accelerating the phaseout already in law; the cleanup-funding-cut figure reported at the committee stage was not confirmed against the final enacted bill's own text or appropriations figures.

The 600,000+ exposed-servicemembers and installation-count figures are pre-existing background scale (from 2022-2023 DOD/EWG data), included for context on what's at stake generally, not as a measurement of this specific rollback's marginal health effect.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the enacted foam purchase/use-deadline extension and the destruction-technology authority replacing the committee-stage full incineration-pause repeal, corroborated across The Hill and Holland & Knight's FY2026 NDAA legal analysis. HIGH confidence the final bill also added a new DOD PFAS-communities Coordinator role, per Rep. Fitzpatrick's own press release. MODERATE-LOW confidence on the cleanup-funding-cut dollar figure, which comes from committee-stage reporting (Guardian/EWG, August-September 2025) and was not independently confirmed against the final enacted bill's own funding tables -- worth re-verifying before citing the specific dollar figure in debate. This entry corrects the original discovery record's framing (a straight 'PFAS rollback' based on August-September 2025 committee-stage reporting) to reflect the mixed final outcome actually signed into law December 18, 2025.

rule_name: One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Rescission of the Neighborhood Access and Equity Transportation Grant Program
agency: Congress / Department of Transportation (Federal Highway Administration)
status: Fully Repealed -- all unobligated program funds rescinded by statute
original_rule_summary: The Neighborhood Access and Equity program, created by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 with $3.2 billion in funding and administered by the Federal Highway Administration, funded local projects to reconnect communities divided by highways, improve walkability and pedestrian/cyclist safety, and build transportation infrastructure in disadvantaged areas -- both Democratic- and Republican-represented districts received awards.
what_changed: As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), Congress rescinded all unobligated funds awarded under the Neighborhood Access and Equity program. Transportation for America found that only about $777 million of the program's $3.2 billion had actually been obligated (contractually committed) by the time of rescission, leaving roughly $2.4 billion in already-awarded but not-yet-obligated grants clawed back -- reported elsewhere as approximately $2.2-3.1 billion depending on the specific accounting window and whether the full program authorization or only the awarded-but-unobligated portion is counted. The cuts hit projects in both parties' districts: in Jacksonville, Florida, a $147 million award (the largest federal grant in the city's history, developed with the Jacksonville Transportation Authority and nonprofit Groundwork Jacksonville) to build new links between urban neighborhoods was rescinded; in St. George, Utah, an $87 million award to build two underpasses relieving chronic traffic congestion caused by an interstate highway dividing the city was rescinded; a $75 million highway-rebuild project in Montana and infrastructure fixes in Kentucky's Bowling Green and rural Maryland were also affected, among 55 total projects nationwide, 19 of them in Republican-held districts. Congressional Republicans and the administration framed the rescission as part of a broader effort to eliminate federal programs using the terms 'equity' or 'DEI,' consistent with Trump's stated initiative against what he called 'radical and wasteful government D.E.I. programs' -- even though the underlying projects were physical road, sidewalk, and underpass infrastructure, not diversity training or personnel programs.

primary_proponent.role: Passed the rescission as part of the broader FY2025 reconciliation act
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally directing this specific rescission; it was adopted as part of the broader OBBBA reconciliation package targeting programs framed as 'equity' initiatives.

estimated_health_impact.summary: The rescinded projects were pedestrian, cyclist, and traffic-safety infrastructure (underpasses to separate pedestrians from highway traffic, walkability improvements) whose loss removes documented safety and mobility improvements from the affected communities, though no source reviewed quantifies a specific injury or mortality impact.

rule_name: Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) Standards, Model Years 2022-2031 ("SAFE Vehicles Rule III")
agency: NHTSA (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration), Department of Transportation
status: Proposed Repeal -- signed/proposed December 2, 2025, published in the Federal Register December 5, 2025; a public hearing was held January 7-8, 2026 and the comment period was extended to February 4, 2026; not yet finalized as of this entry's last verification
original_rule_summary: Biden-era CAFE fuel economy standards for passenger cars and light trucks required the industry fleet average to reach roughly 49.1 mpg by model year 2026, rising to roughly 50.4 mpg by model year 2031.
what_changed: NHTSA's SAFE Vehicles Rule III, proposed December 2, 2025, would cut those requirements to roughly 30.4 mpg (MY2026) and 34.5 mpg (MY2031) -- an approximately 18.7 mpg reduction by 2031 relative to the existing standards -- while also retroactively resetting the MY2022 baseline to 36 mpg for passenger cars and 27.7 mpg for light trucks, excluding the outsized fuel-economy credit electric vehicles previously received; DLA Piper's legal analysis called this an 'unprecedented retroactive change to standards for completed model years' 2022 through 2025, since those vehicles were already manufactured under the old baseline. The proposal also eliminates the inter-manufacturer credit-trading system and revises the light-duty vehicle fleet classification system. Trump announced the proposal at a White House event on December 3, 2025, flanked by Detroit and global automaker executives; Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said the company 'appreciates the Trump Administration's actions to re-align the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards with real world market conditions.' DOT's own projections claim the changes would cut the average new-vehicle sticker price by about $900 by 2031 and save $109 billion in total over five years. Democratic lawmakers opposing the rollback cited estimates of more than 450 additional premature deaths and nearly 14,000 additional asthma exacerbations nationally if finalized, per The Hill's reporting on their public statement; the specific underlying study behind that figure was not independently confirmed in sourcing reviewed for this entry. Two related-but-legally-distinct actions were bundled into contemporaneous coverage of the administration's broader anti-EV push, but are NOT part of this NHTSA rulemaking and don't yet have their own dedicated entries in this tracker: Congress eliminated the federal EV purchase tax credit and moved up the end date of the home EV-charger installation credit via the 2025 reconciliation bill (a legislative action), and separately voted via the Congressional Review Act to revoke the Clean Air Act waivers that had let California set its own zero-emission-vehicle sales mandates.

primary_proponent.name: Sean Duffy
primary_proponent.note: Oversees NHTSA, which proposed the rule; no more specific named NHTSA official was identified in sourcing reviewed as the rule's individual author. See also dot-safety-rule-rollback-blitz-2025.json: same Secretary, same 'slash red tape' framing, but a distinct set of actions (30+ DOT safety-rule rollbacks across sub-agencies, documented separately).

corporate_beneficiaries: Automakers seeking relief from Biden-era fuel-economy compliance costs, including Stellantis, which publicly praised the proposal at its announcement

status: Signed and in effect; implementation underway
date_of_action: 2025-05-23 (executive order signed) through 2026-02 (initial DOE recycling-technology grants awarded)
original_rule_summary: Since the Cold War era, the U.S. has generally pursued a 'dilute and dispose' policy for surplus weapons-grade plutonium -- diluting it with inert material and burying it, rather than reprocessing/recycling it -- specifically to avoid separating out plutonium in a form that could be diverted for weapons use, a nonproliferation safeguard. Commercial spent nuclear fuel from light-water reactors has similarly not been reprocessed domestically for decades, for the same proliferation-risk reasons that led the U.S. to abandon reprocessing in the 1970s.
what_changed: On May 23, 2025, as part of a broader package of nuclear-energy executive orders (including 'Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base'), Trump signed an order directing DOE to halt the surplus-plutonium 'dilute and dispose' program and instead establish a program to process surplus plutonium and make it available for industrial and reactor-fuel use, including for advanced reactor designs and power for AI data centers. The order also directs DOE to develop mechanisms to transfer spent nuclear fuel from commercial light-water reactors to a government-owned, privately operated reprocessing and recycling facility, and to evaluate reprocessing/recycling of DOE- and DoD-managed reactor fuel. On nuclear regulatory structure, the order directs the Secretary of Energy, in consultation with the NRC Chair and OMB Director, to develop a plan to expand domestic uranium conversion and enrichment capacity -- a framework critics say shifts influence over nuclear fuel-cycle decisions toward DOE and the White House relative to the historically independent NRC's safety-focused regulatory role. Implementation proceeded through 2025-2026: DOE issued an RFA in October 2025 to establish a surplus-plutonium industrial-use program, and awarded $19 million in February 2026 to five companies for spent-fuel recycling technology research.

rule_name: One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Accelerated Wind/Solar Tax-Credit Phase-Out, Plus USDA's Cancellation of Farmland Solar/Wind Funding
agency: Congress / Department of the Treasury (tax-credit phase-out); Department of Agriculture (farmland funding cancellation)
status: Fully Enacted (tax-credit phase-out) / Finalized (USDA program changes)
original_rule_summary: The Inflation Reduction Act's clean-energy tax credits (for wind and solar generation, among other technologies) allowed projects placed in service on a multi-year timeline to qualify for federal tax credits, supporting project financing industry-wide. Separately, USDA's Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) and Business and Industry Guaranteed Loan program had provided more than $2 billion in loans and grants supporting solar and wind installations on farmland, including large ground-mount systems.
what_changed: Trump signed H.R. 1, the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' (OBBBA), into law on July 4, 2025 after Senate passage on July 1 and House passage on July 3. The law accelerates the phase-out of wind and solar tax credits: projects must now begin construction by July 5, 2026 and be placed in service by the end of 2027 to qualify, a sharply compressed timeline compared to the prior multi-year phase-out schedule, while a separately-added credit for metallurgical coal used in steelmaking runs with no phase-out through the end of 2029. Reuters and AP reporting characterized the changes as a major setback for renewable-energy project financing, with thousands of already-planned wind and solar projects at risk of losing eligibility if not completed within the new compressed window, alongside separate provisions expanding oil, gas, and coal leasing and blocking a planned methane-emissions penalty. Separately, on August 18-19, 2025, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced USDA would no longer support solar and wind development on productive farmland: ground-mount solar systems larger than 50kW (or those unable to document historical energy usage) became ineligible for REAP's guaranteed-loan program, REAP grants no longer receive priority points for solar/wind projects, solar and wind projects generally became ineligible for the Business and Industry Guaranteed Loan program, and projects containing Chinese-made components or sited on USDA-certified cropland were separately excluded. Rollins justified the change by saying 'our prime farmland should not be wasted and replaced with green new deal subsidized solar panels' and that the projects were 'taking away the futures of the next generation of farmers.' USDA's own prior research undercuts the scale of that claim: a 2024 USDA study found wind turbines and solar farms affected about 424,000 acres of rural land in 2020 -- less than 0.05% of the nearly 900 million acres of U.S. farmland -- and a separate USDA Economic Research Service analysis (Amber Waves, September 2024) found that agricultural land near solar and wind projects usually remained in agricultural production after development, contrary to a wholesale-farmland-loss framing. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0350): the House's own May 22, 2025 passage of the bill (before Senate revisions and the final July 4 enactment) already specified several of the eventually-enacted cuts in the same form -- ending EV tax credits in 2025, phasing out wind, solar, and nuclear power tax breaks by 2032, and eliminating home energy-efficiency subsidies after 2025 -- confirming these provisions were not added or substantially altered between House passage and final enactment. A concrete local example of the law's real-world stakes: Cartersville, Georgia -- in Bartow County, which backed Trump with 75% of the vote across all three of his campaigns -- is home to a $5 billion Hyundai Motor Group/SK On battery factory and a $2.3 billion Qcells solar-panel plant (combined $7.3 billion investment, pledging average wages of $53,000 and thousands of jobs), both of which were financed in part on the strength of the same federal clean-energy subsidies this law curtails; AP reported local officials warned the cuts could jeopardize the area's promised jobs and economic growth despite the town's strong political support for Trump.

rule_name: Federal buyouts to cancel offshore wind leases; DOE Section 202(c) emergency orders forcing aging coal plants to stay online
agency: Department of the Interior (offshore wind leasing); Department of Energy (Section 202(c) emergency orders); Department of the Treasury (buyout payments)
status: Ongoing -- buyouts and emergency coal orders both continuing as of mid-2026
date_of_action: 2025-05 (first DOE Section 202(c) coal emergency orders) through 2026-07 (continued buyouts and coal-plant orders)
original_rule_summary: Offshore wind leases had been awarded and projects were underway (including by TotalEnergies off New York and North Carolina) under normal federal leasing and permitting processes established under prior administrations; separately, aging coal plant operators had scheduled retirements through normal grid-planning and utility-commission processes, coordinated with regional grid operators to ensure adequate replacement capacity.
what_changed: Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0507): the buyout strategy below was the administration's second approach, not its first. In an earlier, more direct phase, Trump officials told a federal court on August 31, 2025 that they would move to vacate approval for US Wind's Maryland offshore project (designed to power an estimated 718,000 homes) by September 12, 2025, following an already-imposed suspension of offshore leasing and a stop-work order on a Rhode Island wind farm. By late September 2025, the administration had halted or moved to cancel nine already-permitted offshore wind projects -- five of them already under construction -- threatening an estimated 9,000 jobs and power for nearly 5 million homes, while separately banning new solar and wind development on federal land and in federal waters and publicly calling clean energy a 'scam.' It was these direct-action attempts that federal courts went on to block, prompting the shift to the buyout strategy described below. After federal courts blocked Trump's attempts to halt offshore wind development through direct executive action, the administration shifted to a buyout strategy: paying developers to voluntarily forfeit already-awarded offshore wind leases. As of mid-2026, buyout agreements have canceled nine future wind farms on the East and West coasts at a cost of roughly $2.7 billion in taxpayer funds. French energy company TotalEnergies forfeited its leases for New York and North Carolina offshore wind projects in exchange for $928 million reimbursing its original lease expenditures -- money TotalEnergies has said it will reinvest into oil and gas projects, including a liquefied natural gas export facility in Texas. Separately, starting in May 2025, the Department of Energy began issuing 90-day emergency orders under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to prevent the retirement of aging coal-fired power plants, overriding operators' own retirement schedules; DOE has used this authority on at least five plants from Michigan to Washington State, including preventing Colorado's Craig Station Unit 1 from retiring one day before its scheduled date. A 2025 Grid Strategies report estimated the cost of keeping these plants open at over $200 million so far, with total ratepayer costs potentially exceeding $3 billion annually if the practice extends to more plants scheduled for retirement before 2028; Mother Jones separately reported the administration has directed roughly $1.1 billion specifically toward extending coal plant life, alongside lowered federal coal royalty rates and expanded coal leasing. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0615): the specific figures behind that royalty/leasing action were reported September 29, 2025 -- Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced the opening of 13 million acres of federal land for coal mining and $625 million to recommission or modernize coal-fired power plants, cutting the federal coal royalty rate from 12.5% to 7%; Burgum called the initiative 'mine, baby, mine,' framing it alongside Trump's 'drill, baby, drill' oil-and-gas push. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0547): the direct-action track this entry documents did not end when the buyout strategy began -- it continued in parallel. The Rhode Island stop-work order referenced above targeted Revolution Wind specifically: an Orsted-owned, $6.2 billion, 704-megawatt project 80% complete (all offshore foundations installed, 45 of 65 turbines up) that would have powered 350,000 homes across Rhode Island and Connecticut, halted by an August 22, 2025 Bureau of Ocean Energy Management order citing unspecified national-security concerns. On January 15/22, 2026, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum expanded this into a broader freeze, pausing five East Coast offshore wind projects -- Vineyard Wind 1 (Massachusetts), Revolution Wind (Rhode Island), Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind/CVOW (Dominion Energy), Sunrise Wind (New York), and Empire Wind 1 (New York) -- citing classified Defense Department reports on 'emerging national security risks.' Burgum later specified the concern publicly: turbine blades and reflective towers allegedly create radar 'clutter' that could obscure detection of 'drone swarms' approaching the East Coast, particularly around New York. Developers and states sued: Orsted and Equinor (Empire Wind 1) filed suit, followed by Dominion Energy on December 23, 2025 over the Virginia project; Connecticut and Rhode Island joined as plaintiffs, arguing the freeze was arbitrary and unconstitutional given the projects' multi-billion-dollar sunk investment. As in the entry's earlier direct-action phase, courts again ruled against the administration: federal judges granted preliminary injunctions allowing Revolution Wind, Empire Wind 1, and the Dominion Virginia project to resume construction while the underlying lawsuits proceeded. Revolution Wind itself came online, delivering power to the New England grid, by March 13, 2026.

status: Proposed Repeal (two linked proposed rules, comment period closed 2026-07-20, public hearing 2026-07-07, not yet finalized)
original_rule_summary: April 2024 EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation -- the first-ever federal limits on PFAS ('forever chemicals') in drinking water -- set legally enforceable Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for six PFAS (PFOA, PFOS, PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA/GenX, and Hazard Index mixtures), with compliance required by 2029. status: N/A for this entry -- it documents an aggregate mortality analysis spanning several already-tracked actions, not the repeal status of any one rule; see the cross-referenced entries below for each underlying action's own status

original_rule_summary: Not applicable in the single-rule sense -- this entry aggregates the projected mortality effect of several distinct 2025 actions, each separately tracked: EPA's March 12, 2025 omnibus deregulatory announcement (see propublica-climate-rollback-heat-death-projection-2025's cross-reference to epa-31-rule-deregulation-announcement-2025.json), the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's repeal of clean-electricity/EV/manufacturing tax credits, easing of coal-plant pollution restrictions, weakened vehicle fuel standards, and expanded oil/gas/mining leasing on federal lands.
what_changed: A ProPublica/Guardian joint analysis (published Nov. 19, 2025) estimated that the combined effect of the above 2025 actions will cause approximately 1.3 million additional heat-related deaths globally between now and roughly 2115. The analysis used Rhodium Group's midrange estimate of 5.7 billion additional metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions attributable to the policies through 2035, applied to the peer-reviewed 'mortality cost of carbon' metric (developed by economist R. Daniel Bressler), under which each roughly 4,434 metric tons of CO2 emitted causes one additional temperature-related death over an 80-year window. The analysis found the burden falls overwhelmingly on poorer, hotter countries that contributed little to historical emissions: the U.S. has produced about 20% of the world's cumulative greenhouse gases with 4% of its population, but is projected to bear only up to about 1% of the temperature-related deaths these specific additional emissions cause. Each individual policy this analysis aggregates over -- the EPA announcement, the OBBBA tax-credit repeal, the vehicle-standards rollback, the drilling/mining expansion -- is tracked in this database's own separate entries; this entry exists specifically to hold the combined, cross-policy mortality estimate the individual entries note has not otherwise been produced (see epa-31-rule-deregulation-announcement-2025.json's own estimated_health_impact caveat, written before this analysis was published).

rule_name: Revocation of SEC Enforcement Division's Delegated Authority to Issue Formal Orders of Investigation and Subpoenas
status: Fully Repealed (the 2009 delegation of authority itself)
original_rule_summary: Since 2009 -- adopted after the financial crisis, specifically to speed up fraud investigations -- the SEC had delegated authority to the Director of the Division of Enforcement to issue formal orders of investigation and the subpoenas that come with them, letting enforcement staff open investigations and compel documents/testimony without a Commission vote for each case.
what_changed: On March 10, 2025, the SEC's Republican majority -- then-Acting Chairman Mark Uyeda and Commissioner Hester Peirce -- voted to revoke the Enforcement Division's delegated authority to issue formal orders of investigation and subpoenas, over the objection of the sole Democratic commissioner, Caroline Crenshaw. The rule returns the SEC to its pre-2009 process, in which a majority of sitting Commissioners must personally approve the opening of any formal investigation and any subpoena issued in connection with it. Law-firm client alerts (Ballard Spahr, Arnold & Porter, Latham) characterized the change as likely to slow the pace and reduce the volume of SEC investigations by adding a bureaucratic approval step to every case. The rule took effect roughly six weeks before Paul Atkins was confirmed and sworn in as SEC Chairman (April 2025); its practical effect became publicly visible a year later when Enforcement Division Director Margaret Ryan abruptly resigned in March 2026 after reportedly being blocked from pursuing fraud charges against Trump- and Musk-linked figures (Justin Sun, Elon Musk) -- see the separate `sec-enforcement-chief-ryan-resignation-2026.json` entry for that downstream episode, which this rule's Commission-approval requirement structurally enabled.

primary_proponent.name: Mark Uyeda
primary_proponent.role: SEC Acting Chairman at the time of the vote
primary_proponent.note: Voted with Commissioner Hester Peirce to adopt the rule by a 2-1 party-line vote, over Commissioner Caroline Crenshaw's dissent.

estimated_health_impact.summary: Concentrating subpoena and investigation-opening authority in a Commission majority vote, rather than career enforcement staff, adds delay and political-approval risk to every SEC investigation -- including ones touching companies or individuals with ties to the administration, as the later Ryan-resignation episode illustrated.

rule_name: 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule ('Roadless Rule')
status: Proposed Repeal (rulemaking in progress; final rule and record of decision expected late 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-06-23 (rescission announced) through 2026-08 (Forest Service formally files proposed repeal; rulemaking ongoing)
original_rule_summary: Finalized in 2001 under the Clinton administration, the Roadless Rule prohibited road construction, road reconstruction, and most timber harvest across roughly 58.5 million acres (nearly a third) of National Forest System land -- the largest single block of federal land-management protection outside the wilderness system -- to preserve undeveloped forest, protect watersheds and wildlife habitat, and limit human-caused wildfire ignition sources associated with roads.
what_changed: On June 23, 2025, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced USDA's intent to rescind the Roadless Rule entirely, opening nearly 59 million acres of national forest to road construction, logging, and mining, framing the repeal as removing an 'impediment to responsible forest management' and citing wildfire-prevention goals. A public comment period on the initial proposal closed in September 2025, drawing 625,957 comments; the nonprofit Center for Western Priorities' review found more than 99% opposed repeal. USDA and the Forest Service continued the rulemaking through 2026: a formal proposed rule and draft environmental review followed, with the Forest Service filing the formal proposed repeal (covering an updated figure of roughly 44.7 million acres in some subsequent framing) in August 2026, opening a further comment period; a final rule and record of decision are expected in late 2026. Notably, the Forest Service's own internal fire analysis -- surfaced during the rulemaking process -- found that wildfire-ignition probability, frequency, and number all increase with road density, and that roadless areas see FEWER wildfire starts than roaded national forest land, directly undercutting the administration's stated fire-prevention rationale for the repeal; the agency's own scientists separately found the repeal could degrade drinking water quality for an estimated 25 million Americans who depend on national-forest watersheds. Firefighters and fire-policy experts, including FUSEE executive director Timothy Ingalsbee, publicly disputed the wildfire-prevention rationale, noting logging roads are built for resource extraction rather than fire suppression and that existing Forest Service road maintenance is already critically underfunded.

primary_proponent.name: Brooke Rollins
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the rescission in a June 23, 2025 USDA press release and has continued to lead the rulemaking process through subsequent 2025-2026 USDA announcements.

corporate_beneficiaries: Timber and logging industry interests seeking access to previously roadless national forest land
Off-road-vehicle and motorized-recreation advocacy groups (e.g., BlueRibbon Coalition), which publicly celebrated the rescission as expanding access

estimated_health_impact.summary: The Forest Service's own scientists found the repeal could degrade drinking water quality for an estimated 25 million Americans who rely on national-forest watersheds, and the agency's own internal fire analysis found road density increases wildfire-ignition probability and frequency -- directly contradicting the administration's stated wildfire-prevention justification for the rule change.

The drinking-water and wildfire-risk findings are drawn from the Forest Service's OWN internal analysis, not an outside advocacy estimate, which is unusually strong sourcing for a health-impact claim in this tracker but should still be presented as the agency's own scientific finding being in tension with its political leadership's stated rationale, not as an independently adjudicated fact.

rule_name: Salmonella Framework for Raw Poultry Products (withdrawal)
status: Fully Withdrawn
original_rule_summary: In August 2024, FSIS proposed a new regulatory framework declaring raw chicken and turkey products "adulterated" -- and therefore subject to recall or sale-block -- if they contained 10 or more colony-forming units of Salmonella per gram/milliliter and tested positive for one of several Salmonella serotypes linked to human illness. It was the first proposal to treat Salmonella contamination itself, above a set threshold, as grounds for regulatory action on raw poultry, rather than relying solely on post-market illness surveillance. FSIS estimated the framework would meaningfully reduce Salmonella-attributed illness from chicken and turkey.
what_changed: On April 25, 2025, FSIS withdrew the proposed Salmonella framework in its entirety, stating it would "further assess its approach for addressing Salmonella illnesses associated with poultry products" rather than finalize the 2024 proposal. The agency's withdrawal notice followed roughly 7,000 public comments, including opposition from poultry and meat industry groups, members of Congress, and a risk-assessment firm retained by industry that challenged the proposed testing thresholds. No replacement framework or timeline for a new proposal was announced.

primary_proponent.name: Brooke Rollins
primary_proponent.note: FSIS, which she oversees, issued the formal withdrawal notice; no more specific individual within FSIS is named on the record as having personally driven the decision.

corporate_beneficiaries: Poultry and meat processing industry -- trade groups and a risk-assessment consultancy retained by industry were among the roughly 7,000 commenters whose opposition the withdrawal notice cited

estimated_health_impact.summary: FSIS's own data attributes well over 100,000 Salmonella illnesses per year to chicken and turkey consumption; the withdrawn framework was the first proposal to regulate Salmonella contamination itself (rather than only post-illness surveillance) on raw poultry, and its withdrawal leaves that regulatory gap unaddressed with no announced replacement.

rule_name: VA fiduciary-based firearm-purchase prohibition, and related mental-illness firearm restrictions, as part of a nearly three-dozen-rule ATF/DOJ gun-regulation rollback
status: Finalized (VA fiduciary rule, February 2026) / Rolling proposed and final actions (DOJ/ATF's 34-rule regulatory package under Executive Order 14206, released April 29, 2026, with individual rules proceeding through notice-and-comment on separate timelines through at least October 2026)
date_of_action: 2026-02 (VA fiduciary rule change) through 2026-07 (DOJ/ATF rollback package target date)
original_rule_summary: Under a rule dating to the Obama administration, veterans who require a VA-appointed fiduciary to manage their benefits because they have been deemed unable to manage their own affairs -- including for certain mental-illness-related determinations -- were reported to the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) as a prohibited category for firearm purchases, a restriction Congress had already partially curtailed via a 2017 Congressional Review Act resolution.
what_changed: In February 2026, the Department of Veterans Affairs removed the requirement that veterans needing a fiduciary to manage their VA benefits be reported to NICS as prohibited firearm purchasers, restoring gun-purchase eligibility to veterans who have been formally found unable to manage their own financial affairs. This was one piece of a broader Washington Post-documented effort in which DOJ unveiled plans to eliminate or revise more than three dozen firearms regulations -- including rules restricting sales to people with documented mental illness and rules governing private weapons transfers -- while DOGE separately sent staff into ATF with a mandate to revise or eliminate more than 50 rules and gun restrictions by July 4, 2026. Senior DOJ officials described the changes collectively as cutting 'unnecessary government bureaucracy without risking public safety'; gun-safety groups objected specifically to the mental-illness and fiduciary-status rollbacks as removing an existing, narrowly targeted safeguard. Re-verified 2026-08-16: DOJ and ATF's broader package has since been more precisely documented -- released April 29, 2026 under Executive Order 14206 as a 34-rule reform package (not the ~36 figure originally reported), proceeding through individual notice-and-comment rulemakings on rolling timelines rather than a single July 4, 2026 finalization. Confirmed individual pieces include repeal of the Biden-era 'zero tolerance' dealer-penalty policy, a new federal gun-rights restoration system, narrowed 'unlawful drug user' and 'fugitive from justice' definitions, and (proposed July 3, 2026, comment through October 5, 2026) reduced fingerprinting requirements on certain firearms applications. This confirms the package is real and substantial, though this entry's original focus -- the mental-illness/fiduciary-status and private-transfer provisions specifically -- was not independently re-confirmed as finalized in this pass; it remains sourced to the original Washington Post reporting. Re-verified 2026-08-22: the mental-illness provision within the broader DOJ/ATF package -- flagged in the prior recheck as not independently re-confirmed beyond the original Washington Post reporting -- is now specifically documented. ATF published a proposed rule on May 8, 2026 (RIN 1140-AB04) revising the regulatory definitions of "adjudicated as a mental defective" and "committed to a mental institution," the two categories that trigger a federal firearm-purchase prohibition on mental-health grounds. The proposal would narrow both definitions to require a formal legal adjudication or commitment process (notice, hearing, counsel, opportunity to contest) rather than an emergency hold, clinical judgment, or administrative form alone. Its comment period closed August 6, 2026; gun-violence-prevention groups Giffords and Brady submitted a joint opposition comment, and the rule had not been finalized as of this recheck.

The broader DOJ/ATF package's legal basis has since been identified as Executive Order 14206 (April 29, 2026 package release), still with no single named individual driving day-to-day implementation identified in reporting reviewed.

rule_name: Waters of the United States (WOTUS) Narrowing — Post-Sackett Redefinition
status: Proposed Repeal (comment period on original Nov. 2025 proposal closed 2026-01-05; EPA has since sent a supplemental proposed rule to OMB for review as of late June 2026, reopening comment on revised aspects rather than proceeding to finalize -- not yet finalized)
original_rule_summary: The 'waters of the United States' (WOTUS) definition determines which streams, wetlands, and other water bodies are protected under the Clean Water Act. Following the Supreme Court's 2023 Sackett v. EPA decision, the Biden administration issued a 2023 rule conforming WOTUS to Sackett's narrower 'relatively permanent' and 'continuous surface connection' standards.
what_changed: EPA and the Army Corps proposed a further narrowing of the 2023 rule -- the sixth WOTUS redefinition in a decade -- including removing 'interstate waters' from the definition entirely and tightening the definitions of 'continuous surface connection' and 'relatively permanent waters.' The stated aim is to end a split implementation (the 2023 rule is currently enjoined in 26 states) and further reduce federal permitting jurisdiction. Re-verified 2026-08-16: rather than proceeding to finalize the November 2025 proposal after its January 5, 2026 comment period closed, EPA sent a second, supplemental proposed rule to OMB for interagency review around June 30, 2026, revising unspecified aspects of the original proposal and seeking renewed public comment -- an unusual procedural step per InsideEPA.com and E&E News/POLITICO coverage. This substantially delays the final rule beyond the 'roughly mid-2026' timeline legal analysts had previously projected; no publication date for the supplemental proposal in the Federal Register was found as of this update.

primary_proponent.note: EPA and the Army jointly proposed the rule; Zeldin is the named agency head across the broader 2025-2026 EPA deregulatory push.

title: Energy Secretary Wright Threatens U.S. Withdrawal From the International Energy Agency Over Its Climate Modeling, Prompting the Agency to Soften Its Forecasts
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition -- ultimatum issued Feb. 2026 with a stated one-year deadline; the U.S. has not withdrawn from the IEA, but the agency has already altered its public forecasting in apparent response
what_changed: At the IEA's 2026 Ministerial Meeting in Paris, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright delivered a one-year ultimatum demanding the International Energy Agency abandon its 'net-zero' climate-transition modeling and pivot toward a traditional energy-security framing, warning the U.S. would use 'all the pressure we have' to force the change or reconsider its IEA membership. Wright accused countries prioritizing net-zero goals of committing 'economic suicide' and criticized IEA's scenario modeling as based on 'climate ambitions' rather than 'energy data.' The Paris meeting notably ended without a joint communique, underscoring the depth of the U.S.-IEA rift. In apparent response, the IEA subsequently softened its public forecasting, signaling a shift toward projecting continued oil-demand growth through mid-century rather than its prior net-zero-aligned trajectory -- a substantive change in the independent international agency's own published analysis following direct U.S. political pressure.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright
primary_proponent.note: Wright's stated rationale is that IEA's net-zero-oriented modeling misrepresents actual energy-market data and disadvantages fossil-fuel-producing nations, including the U.S.

estimated_impact.summary: An international energy-data agency long relied upon for independent, non-political demand and supply forecasting altered its public analysis following a direct U.S. political ultimatum -- a documented instance of political pressure producing a substantive change in an ostensibly technical/independent international body's output, distinct from and more concrete than an unexercised private threat.
estimated_impact.caveat: The U.S. has not actually withdrawn from the IEA as of this entry's addition -- Wright's ultimatum carries a stated one-year deadline, and IEA's forecast shift, while reported as connected, was not accompanied by an explicit IEA statement confirming the U.S. pressure as the specific cause.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on Wright's ultimatum, its specific terms, and the absence of a joint communique -- corroborated across CNBC, Washington Examiner, and Euronews. MODERATE confidence on the direct causal link between Wright's pressure and IEA's subsequent forecast softening, since IEA did not explicitly attribute the change to U.S. pressure in sourcing reviewed, though the timing and outlets' own characterization support the connection. Rechecked 2026-09-08 (visitor-flagged update request) -- no material change; IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026, the concrete test of whether the net-zero scenario is actually dropped from the annual flagship report, is not due until October 2026, and the U.S. has not withdrawn from the IEA. The Energy Mix's Feb. 22, 2026 reporting on the same Paris ministerial (IEA omitting climate from its stated priorities list, Birol declining to commit to a future net-zero scenario) corroborates this entry's account but describes the same Feb. 19 event already documented here, not a new development.
